Health & disease Diseases Avian influenza Iowa State University's H5N1 study highlights need for broader livestock surveillance Researchers say more monitoring is needed after finding mammary glands of several livestock species could harbor avian influenza 12 August 2026 2 minute read By: Iowa State University North America An ongoing outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza has affected more than 184 million domestic poultry since 2022 and, since making the leap to dairy cattle in spring 2024, more than 1,000 milking cow herds. A new study led by Iowa State University researchers shows that the mammary glands of several other production animals – including pigs, sheep, goats, beef cattle and alpacas – are biologically suitable to harbor avian influenza, due to high levels of sialic acids. “The main thing we wanted to understand in this study is whether there is potential for transmission among these other domestic mammals and humans, and it looks like there is,” said Rahul Nelli, the study’s lead author and a research assistant professor of veterinary diagnostic and production animal medicine. Sialic acid, a sugar molecule found on the surface of many types of animal cells, provides an influenza virus the microscopic docking station it needs to infect a host cell, an entry point for attaching and invading. A study by many of the same researchers last year found that dairy cattle udders have high levels of sialic acid, which helped explain why the H5N1 avian influenza outbreak was able to spread rapidly among dairy herds. In the study published Nov. 27 in the Journal of Dairy Science, a research team that includes scientists from the ISU College of Veterinary Medicine and the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Animal Disease Center in Ames also found the same receptors in the mammary glands of the humans. Only a few sporadic cases of H5N1 infection have been reported in the animals examined in the new study, but those species aren’t being tested on a widespread basis, said Dr. Todd Bell, professor of veterinary pathology and a study co-author. “If we don’t look, we don’t know,” Bell said. In dairy herds, H5N1 infections are causing sick cows to produce milk contaminated with the virus, prompting nationwide surveillance testing of raw cow milk samples by the USDA. Pasteurization kills influenza viruses, so store-bought milk is safe. But concerns about raw milk should extend to other mammalian livestock, Nelli said. “Some people do consume the raw milk of these other animals,” he said. The presence of the virus in milk from infected cows has likely played a role in the H5N1 spreading and makes transmission to humans a bigger risk, Nelli said. “If a virus in livestock is being spread by respiratory infections, few humans will be in close enough contact to catch it. But milk is an entirely different situation because it’s transported into communities,” he said. All of the mammary gland tissues examined in the new study had sialic acid receptors preferred by both avian influenza and the seasonal influenza that circulates more readily among humans. The possibility of both types of viruses comingling and transmitting between different species heightens concerns about more dangerous adaptations emerging, Bell said. H5N1 has in the past had a fatality rate in humans of around 50%, though the 71 confirmed human infections during the current outbreak have led to just two deaths. “We need to try to stay ahead of this so it doesn’t have a chance to continue to replicate and potentially evolve into something even more troublesome,” he said. analysis.time: Published 11 August 2026; study findings reported 12 August 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: United States (Iowa State University-led study); North America; livestock species including dairy cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, beef cattle, and alpacas; human populations consuming raw milk.
analysis.event: A peer-reviewed study led by Iowa State University researchers found that mammary glands of multiple livestock species possess sialic acid receptors that make them biologically suitable hosts for avian influenza, including H5N1. The study highlights potential transmission risks to humans via raw milk and calls for broader livestock surveillance.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Ongoing H5N1 outbreak: over 184 million domestic poultry affected since 2022; more than 1,000 milking cow herds infected since spring 2024. Only sporadic H5N1 cases reported in examined animals; human infections during current outbreak: 71 confirmed with 2 deaths. Pasteurized milk is safe; raw milk from infected cows may be contaminated. Risk of viral reassortment between avian and seasonal influenza in mammals heightens concerns about dangerous adaptations.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: USDA conducting nationwide surveillance testing of raw cow milk samples. Study authors emphasize the need for expanded testing in other mammalian livestock due to undetected infections. Pasteurization inactivates influenza viruses. Current status: under investigation with calls to 'stay ahead' of potential evolution. Unresolved: extent of H5N1 presence in non-dairy livestock and human transmission risk via raw milk from other species.

analysis.brief_en: A new Iowa State University-led study published on 12 August 2026 reveals that mammary glands in multiple livestock species—including pigs, sheep, goats, beef cattle, and alpacas—contain receptors that make them biologically suitable hosts for avian influenza viruses such as H5N1. Researchers warn that undetected infections in these animals could facilitate viral spread to humans, particularly through raw milk consumption, as pasteurization remains the only confirmed safeguard. The findings come amid an ongoing H5N1 outbreak affecting over 1,000 U.S. dairy herds since 2024 and more than 184 million poultry since 2022, with 71 human cases and two deaths reported globally. The study underscores the urgent need for broader livestock surveillance to prevent potential viral reassortment and the emergence of more dangerous strains.

More than 230 cases have been confirmed nationwide, while Australia recorded its first mass wildlife mortality event linked to the virus last week, according to ABC News. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the vaccination campaign would begin across states and territories in the coming days. “We cannot stop the H5 bird flu spreading amongst wild birds, but we can take action to protect the species most at risk and vaccination is now part of that response,” Collins said. Authorities will determine which species are vaccinated based on their vulnerability to the virus and the potential impact on conservation. Environment Minister Murray Watt said widespread vaccination of wild birds was impractical because the vaccine requires two doses, although authorities could vaccinate wild birds where feasible. The government has secured an initial 2 million Australian dollars ($1.3 million) worth of vaccines. Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson cautioned that vaccination was “not a standalone solution,” stressing that biosecurity measures remained crucial. Tasmania, the Northern Territory and the Australian Capital Territory remain the only jurisdictions without confirmed cases. news.content: Home About Clinical Authors Most read this year GP Opinion Videos & Podcasts Professional Comments policy RACGP poll Menu Search for: Advertising newsGP > Clinical Jo Roberts 12 Aug 2026 News Bird flu threat ‘very low’ for humans: CSIRO Jo Roberts 12/08/2026 3:47:12 PM Australia’s H5N1 outbreak is prompting vigilance among authorities, but experts say human transmission risk remains low. The risk of H5N1 transmission from birds to humans ‘remains very low’, says CSIRO experts. Experts from the CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness (ACDP) say the threat of the H5N1 bird flu spreading to humans remains ‘very low’, following Australia’s first recorded mass bird mortality event last week. It comes as the Federal Government moves to vaccinate all native birds in captivity and Victorian authorities prepare to vaccinate around 5000 little penguins at Phillip Island and St Kilda, in an effort to stem the predicted mass mortalities. H5N1 had been detected in every continent except Australia and greater Oceania until June, when the first Australian case was confirmed in a brown skua seabird in Western Australia. ACDP Director Dr Debbie Eagles said for GPs, most guidance would come from epidemiological information. ‘That might be that people present with flu-like symptoms and report exposure to wild birds that have been sick, potentially ones that have tested positive,’ she said. ‘So, people who have been involved in what might be considered high-risk activities, such as direct contact with sick or wild birds.’ She said the whole genome sequence testing the ACDP conducts ‘can help identify the source of the virus, identify changes as we get more detections, can help characterise local transmission events and look for reassortment with influenza viruses that are already circulating in Australian birds.’ ACDP Senior Research Scientist Dr Frank Wong confirmed there has not been any recorded human cases of the disease in Australia related to this outbreak. He said an ‘ecological perfect storm’ would be required for the virus to spill over, but that did not mitigate the need to stay on high alert. Dr Wong added that most recorded cases in humans have presented as mild respiratory infections and/or conjunctivitis, with just two being more severe illness ‘and they were linked to people who were either elderly or had predisposing conditions’. ‘The risk is very low and remains very low for transmission between birds and people. And that’s what we’ve seen internationally over the last few years with this strain,’ he said. He said since 2024–25, there was a spike in human infections in the United States, the majority linked to infected dairy farms, and two outbreaks in poultry farms. ‘Exposure is with people in professions that expose themselves to outbreak environments,’ Dr Wong said. However, he stressed that they were from a different genotype to the H5N1 virus that is seen in Australia. ‘To date, there’s no clear predictor for the ability of these viruses to jump from birds to mammals, and from birds and mammals to humans,’ Dr Wong said. ‘Even in cases where we’ve found the virus in either mammals or humans, the majority of the viruses that are isolated from these cases, it’s still very much an avian-adapted virus, with the majority avian genetic signatures.’ He said people in high-risk occupations ‘should get vaccinated with the standard flu vaccine’ A recent British study of 428 people working with, or exposed to, birds infected with influenza A (H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses (primarily poultry sites), found low rates of human infection among participants. Beginning in 2023, the original study cohort included only asymptomatic people exposed to infected birds, while those with respiratory symptoms were recruited from January 2024 onwards. Less than 1% of participants met the study’s criteria for infection, resulting in two confirmed cases and one unclear case. No severe illness was reported; two of the six PCR-positive participants had mild symptoms. Full personal protective equipment was worn by 85% of participants, who self-reported consistent use, with no breaches, while within the biosecurity area. Only 19% reported having received an influenza vaccination. The researchers noted that although seasonal influenza vaccines do not offer protection to humans against zoonotic influenza, ‘they should be considered for those occupationally exposed to zoonotic influenza to reduce the risk of co-infection and thus reassortment events’. analysis.event: Australian health authorities and CSIRO experts assess the risk of H5N1 avian influenza transmission from birds to humans as 'very low' following Australia’s first recorded mass bird mortality event. The event is reported as under investigation with ongoing monitoring.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: No human cases of H5N1 linked to the current Australian outbreak have been recorded. Internationally, most human H5N1 cases have been mild respiratory infections or conjunctivitis; severe cases were linked to elderly individuals or those with predisposing conditions. GPs are advised to rely on epidemiological information for guidance, particularly for patients with flu-like symptoms and bird exposure.

analysis.brief_en: Australian experts from the CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness (ACDP) have assessed the risk of H5N1 avian influenza transmission from birds to humans as 'very low' following the country’s first recorded mass bird mortality event in August 2026. No human cases linked to the outbreak have been detected, and most international human H5N1 cases have been mild, with severe cases confined to elderly or predisposed individuals. Authorities are vaccinating captive native birds and approximately 5,000 little penguins in Victoria to mitigate predicted mortalities. Whole-genome sequencing is underway to track viral changes and local transmission, while GPs are advised to monitor patients with flu-like symptoms and bird exposure. Seasonal influenza vaccination is recommended for high-risk occupational groups to reduce co-infection risks, though it does not confer protection against zoonotic strains.

news.content_zh: 自 2026 年 8 月该国首次记录到大规模鸟类 死亡率 事件后,澳大利亚联邦科学与工业研究组织 (CSIRO) 澳大利亚疾病预防中心 (ACDP) 的专家评估了 H5N1 禽流感 传播 从鸟类传播到人类的风险“非常低”。尚未发现与 暴发 有关的人类病例,大多数国际人类 H5N1 病例均为轻度病例,严重病例仅限于老年人或易感人群。当局正在维多利亚州为圈养的本土鸟类和大约 5,000 只小企鹅接种疫苗,以降低预计的死亡率。全 基因组 测序正在进行中,以追踪病毒变化和局部 传播,同时建议全科医生监测有流感样症状和鸟类接触的患者。季节性流感 疫苗接种 建议高危职业群体使用,以降低混合感染风险,但它不能提供针对人畜共患菌株的保护。

news.content: Despite intense exposure at poultry outbreak sites, human H5N1 infections were uncommon and mild, reinforcing the value of PPE while underscoring the need for continued surveillance as the virus evolves. A cohort study of persons exposed to highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) at premises with infected animals, England, 2023 to 2025. Image Credit: Dejan Dundjerski / Shutterstock A recent cohort study found low rates of human infection with highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b among workers exposed to infected birds at outbreak premises, with most participants reporting the use of protective equipment. The study was published in the journal Eurosurveillance. Background From 2020 onwards, the number of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A infections among birds has increased, accompanied by corresponding increases in mammalian spillover events. This phenomenon has crossed continents, though the greatest number of cases have been in Europe and the Americas. However, this might reflect limited surveillance and reporting elsewhere, according to the authors. Between 2003 and 2009, there were 468 reported HPAI A(H5N1) cases, with 60% being fatal. In fact, zoonotic A(H5N1) spillover infections have historically been associated with severe illness in humans. In the UK, the 2024/25 avian influenza season saw 81 outbreaks of HPAI A(H5N1). These have often been dealt with by culling and mandatory housing orders to protect public and animal health. Continued circulation and evolution of the virus could increase the risk of mutations that enable human-to-human transmission, a major step towards a pandemic, given the lack of population immunity. Human infection with the current clade 2.3.4.4b was rare until 2024, when the B3.13 genotype emerged in dairy cattle in the USA, followed by the D1.1 genotype. Regular sequencing in the UK has so far found no known reassortment between UK-circulating genotypes and North American strains. There have been no known instances of human-to-human transmission of the 2.3.4.4b clade, but mild infections may still go unrecognized. These could promote viral adaptation to human hosts. Therefore, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends testing of asymptomatic individuals with high-risk contact with infected poultry or potentially contaminated environments. The current study was conducted between April 2023 and March 2025. It aimed to assess the risk posed by avian influenza to human health, including the occurrence and frequency of such infections in exposed individuals, risk factors, and infection characteristics. Study characteristics The study cohort originally included only asymptomatic individuals exposed to infected birds, while those with respiratory symptoms were recruited from January 2024 onwards. It involved 34 infected premises, with 18 remote and 16 in-person recruitments. At these sites, of the 862 exposed people, 428 were recruited, including 68 recruited at multiple sites. In-person recruitment was more successful than remote recruitment, an important point given that recruitment becomes difficult during an ongoing outbreak. Most of the included sites were poultry sites, and one was an animal rescue site. Of the 428 participants, 178 were from the Yorkshire and Humber regions. The median participant age was 37 years, with 69% male. Most were involved in culling, with half employed by the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) and just under half by contractors. Self-collected nasopharyngeal swabs were tested by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for the influenza A M gene. Influenza A-positive samples were subtyped for H5, and all samples were tested for influenza B and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). H5-positive samples underwent confirmatory testing, including whole-genome sequencing and viral culture when possible. Preventive measures The researchers found that 85% of participants reported consistent full personal protective equipment (PPE) use, with no breaches, while within the biosecurity area. During culling, around 98% of APHA and contractor staff, but only 27% of farmers or farm workers, used full PPE. We recommend - Clinical Management of Patients With Relapsed/Refractory Multiple Myeloma Treated With TalquetamabChari A, et al. Clin Lymphoma Myeloma Leuk, 2024. About 86% of participants were exposed to infected birds within two meters. Separately, 81% touched infected birds or their tissues, and 62% touched bird waste, including litter or eggs. Contractors were most likely to touch birds or their tissues, while farmers or their workers were most likely to touch bird waste. Risk of infection While 96% of participants provided a day 0 sample, this declined steadily to 79% on day 8. Only six participants were PCR-positive for influenza A(H5), but only three met the defined criteria for A(H5N1) infection. Of these, two were classified as confirmed cases, while the third was classified as unclear due to sample date issues. The other three detections were classified as being of "uncertain significance" and were suspected to reflect transient mucosal contamination rather than infection. Thus, fewer than 1% of participants met the study's criteria for infection, resulting in 2 confirmed cases and 1 unclear case. No severe illness was reported; two of the six PCR-positive participants had mild symptoms. Among the six PCR-positive individuals, two did not wear full PPE during exposure. All six had touched infected birds, and four had contact with bird waste. PPE use among PCR-positive participants Overall, 3% of those exposed without PPE were PCR-positive, compared with 1% of those reporting PPE use; however, not all PCR-positive participants met the criteria for confirmed infection. Prophylaxis and infection risk None of the six individuals who tested positive had been vaccinated against the flu or had taken antiviral medication prior to the test. Among participants with negative PCR results, 85% reported full PPE use, 20% had received seasonal influenza vaccination, and 3% were on or had recently taken antiviral medication to prevent infection. Human-to-human transmission risk No cases of human-to-human transmission were identified despite contact tracing of the six PCR-positive individuals. Prevention of HPAI in humans The results underline the importance of PPE use while ensuring an adequate distance from infected birds. The occurrence of PCR positivity in humans despite reported full PPE use suggests potential challenges with correct PPE donning and doffing, unrecognized breaches, or compliance in these environments. The authors also discuss the need for a broader public health response. In this study, the response benefited from avian influenza being a notifiable infection with established communication routes, but this might not be the case for non-notifiable zoonotic influenza. For instance, pigs express receptors for both avian and mammalian influenza viruses, creating opportunities for genetic reassortment during coinfection. Outdoor rearing may also expose pigs to wild birds, thereby increasing the risk of coinfection. Similarly, the authors argue for wider environmental surveillance in the vicinity of infected premises to better detect emerging strains. Seasonal flu shots do not protect against zoonotic influenza, but they could reduce the risk of coinfection with seasonal influenza and, by doing so, lower the opportunities for reassortment. The authors discuss the possibility of seasonal vaccination for occupationally exposed people. Unlike seasonal influenza vaccines, H5-specific vaccines are also being considered for people at occupational risk. The US and some European countries have begun acquiring H5N1 vaccines for human use, with Finland piloting vaccination among occupationally exposed people. Poultry vaccination has also been implemented nationally in France. Limitations Self-reported PPE use and the potential for unrecognized failures in PPE use might have reduced the reliability of the data. The study was smaller than originally planned due to resource constraints. Recruitment was also hampered by the lack of financial security if the participants tested positive and had to go into isolation. Demographic data were not obtained from all participants, limiting the generalizability. However, the largest proportion of contractors lived in the most deprived areas, and contractors had the highest proportion exposed by touch, while the majority of APHA staff lived in the three least deprived quintiles. Conclusions Taken together, the study findings suggested a low risk of zoonotic infection and severe disease due to the influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses in exposed individuals under the conditions studied. However, apparent mucosal contamination occurred in some cases despite self-reported full PPE use. All positives were linked to direct exposure, with no secondary transmission. The use of full PPE is an important protective strategy, but could be impractical given the long working hours and extreme conditions during culling operations, for example. Chemoprophylaxis may offer an additional preventive option in some exposure settings, but further study is needed to establish its utility and acceptability, given its potential side effects and limited evidence. The authors emphasize the need to maintain biosecurity standards at the highest level. This includes communicating risk and control measures to all workers and ensuring compliance. Enhanced surveillance should be resumed following identification of an increased risk of animal-to-human transmission, to help mitigate the risks posed by H5N1 in poultry outbreak settings. - Halford, F., Blomquist, P. B., Bray, N., et al. (2026). A cohort study of persons exposed to highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) at premises with infected animals, England, 2023 to 2025. Eurosurveillance. Out of 428 participants, only 2 were confirmed cases and 1 was unclear, with most participants reporting consistent use of personal protective equipment (PPE). The study noted that 85% of participants used PPE, and no severe illness or human-to-human transmission was identified. The researchers emphasized the importance of PPE and adequate distance from infected birds to prevent infections. The study was published in Eurosurveillance and highlighted the need for continued surveillance and a broader public health response. The findings suggest a low risk of zoonotic infection and severe disease under the studied conditions.

analysis.brief_en: Researchers have developed a potential vaccine to protect cattle from bird flu, as reported by The Cattle Site on 10 August 2026. The vaccine strategy is designed to target multiple H5N1 strains, aiming to reduce the impact of the disease on cattle operations and agricultural systems. This development is part of broader efforts to enhance livestock surveillance and prevention measures. The report highlights the importance of monitoring livestock for signs of avian influenza, particularly in regions like Wales and England where cases have been rising. While the vaccine is a promising advancement, no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are provided. The study is based on research conducted by Iowa State University, which emphasizes the need for increased monitoring of livestock for avian influenza. The information is current as of the publication date and does not indicate any ongoing outbreak or confirmed cases in cattle herds.

The report highlights the importance of monitoring livestock for signs of avian influenza, particularly in regions like Wales and England where cases have been rising. While the vaccine is a promising advancement, no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are provided. The study is based on research conducted by Iowa State University, which emphasizes the need for increased monitoring of livestock for avian influenza. The information is current as of the publication date and does not indicate any ongoing outbreak or confirmed cases in cattle herds.

news.content: Australia to roll out bird flu vaccines for most vulnerable native birds 3 days ago Lana Lam Sydney Getty Images Australia was the last continent to report cases of the highly contagious H5N1 strain Australia will roll out bird flu vaccines in the "coming days and weeks" with native species and birds in captivity first in line for protection from the deadly disease. On Tuesday, the government said that it had AU$2m ($1.4m, £1m) worth of vaccinations for the H5N1 strain - about 1,500 vials - with states and territories to manage the rollout. Australia reported its first case of the highly contagious strain in June, making it the last continent to be impacted. Since then, more than 230 cases have been confirmed. Last week, it saw its first mass mortality from bird flu, with about 50 greater crested terns killed by the disease on an island off the coast of South Australia. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said that while it could not stop the spread of outbreak as it worsened, the programme would target "priority species" most vulnerable to bird flu. The risk to humans remained low, Collins said, and there was no evidence that the disease had impacted the poultry or agriculture sectors. She said while little could be done to stop the spread among wild birds and across the country, "we can take action to protect the species most at risk". "The first vaccines are expected to roll out in coming days and weeks based on an agreed national approach to the targeted vaccination of priority native bird species," she said. "Australians should expect to see more spread and larger numbers, particularly of dead birds and mass mortalities around the country from the H5 bird flu." Environment Minister Murray Watt said birds would each need two doses and that the outbreak was a "serious event". Earlier this month, the government released a list assessing the risk level of bird flu for more than 2,000 of the country's unique native birds and mammals, based on their vulnerability and susceptibility. A handful of species were identified as facing possible extinction while hundreds of others may suffer a "severe reduction" in populations. The program targets priority species most vulnerable to bird flu, and the outbreak is described as a serious event. The risk to humans remains low, and the spread among wild birds is expected to continue.

news.content: Skip to main content Skip to news navigation, settings and search Explore the ABC More from ABC Close menuABC ABC News ABC iview ABC listen Kids & Students Indigenous Information & Services news iview listen Loading ABC News Just In For You Politics World Business Analysis Sport Lifestyle Entertainment Quizzes More Search News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ABC News News Home Bird keepers call for vaccines as bird flu detected inland in South Australia ShareShare article Bird keepers call for vaccines as bird flu detected inland in South Australia By Liz Rymill ABC South East SA Topic:Avian Influenza Posted Fri 14 Aug 2026 at 11:10amFri 14 Aug 2026 at 11:10amFri 14 Aug 2026 at 11:10am Louise McKay is worried about her birds, including her masked owl. (ABC South East SA: Liz Rymill) In short: Backyard bird keepers are calling for vaccines to be made available to protect at-risk species and privately owned birds as avian influenza spreads inland. There have been reports of new cases more than 100 kilometres inland from Robe in South Australia, which has been a focal point of Australia's bird flu outbreak. What's next? The South Australian government says it is part of a national approach using vaccinations to protect some of the most vulnerable native birds. Wildlife experts are calling for vaccines to be made available to backyard bird keepers to protect flocks from avian influenza as the deadly virus spreads inland in some parts of Australia. Wildlife educators Al and Louise McKay, who live 1 kilometre from a virus detection site in regional South Australia, said they were on high alert and worried about their rare birds. The couple lives in the Penola district, about 100 kilometres inland from the tourist town of Robe, which has been a focal point of Australia's bird flu outbreak. Louise and Al McKay are calling for vaccines to be available to backyard bird keepers. (ABC South East SA: Liz Rymill) They are looking at the potential of vaccinating two main species kept under licence: the glossy black cockatoo and the masked owl. In South Australia, this particular species of glossy black cockatoo is critically endangered and only found on Kangaroo Island. "We're very concerned," Mr McKay said. "We want to be proactive and not caught on the back foot. "Our birds are difficult to rehouse and need certain conditions, including light, so vaccinating would be a more practical measure." Louise McKay has modified enclosures to expand biosecurity measures. (ABC South East SA: Liz Rymill) The couple, who run an educational wildlife business that exhibits at aged care homes, schools, country shows and public events, said they would also look at changing their exhibitions and keeping their birds off the program until vaccinations were available. Mrs McKay said they had implemented biosecurity measures, including moving water bowls so they could not be accessed by wild birds, and checking regularly for droppings and for wild birds landing on enclosures. "A lot of bird keepers are anxious about this evolving situation," Mrs McKay said. "Making vaccines available would alleviate some of the stress and provide some assurance our treasured animals are safe." Cases spike along coast H5N1 bird flu has been detected in crested terns along the Limestone Coast, from Robe to Port MacDonnell and Southend. Multiple dead birds can be seen lying on beaches and foreshores at these coastal towns. A dead seagull was found near the Robe boat ramp last week. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine) "We've never seen a crested tern in our area, but I'm told they fly to Lake Mundi and sometimes on the Glenelg River in Victoria," Mr McKay said. Another greater crested tern was also found this week inland at Tarpeena, while across the border in Victoria, a further seven cases of H5N1 bird flu have been detected in greater crested terns in Phillip Island, Mildura, Warrnambool, Hamilton, Hawkesdale and St Andrews Beach. Agriculture Victoria chief biodiversity officer James Todd said the detections in new parts of the state, including at Seal Rocks on Phillip Island, were significant developments. "These detections show us that the virus is continuing to move through wild bird populations, and its ability to move across large regions," he said. A South Australian government spokesperson this week said South Australia was part of a national approach using vaccinations to protect some of the most vulnerable native birds. The spokesperson said the focus would be on "priority species in captivity". They said it was "difficult" and "impractical" to deliver vaccines to most "free-living species" because many vaccines required multiple doses. "Vaccination is another tool which we add to our range of preparedness strategies including surveillance, biosecurity measures and conservation actions to reduce other threats and disturbance — to help protect our wildlife," the spokesperson said. Community has role to play Mrs McKay encouraged community members to continue reporting and recording potential avian influenza cases and to be vigilant around sick birds. She said the infected bird they reported near their home "did attempt to flutter but couldn't get any elevation, was walking in circles, looking down, and wasn't able to move any great distance". Greater crested terns are some of the first birds to have contracted the H5N1 bird flu virus in Australia. (iNaturalist: Tommy Osborne, Greater crested tern, CC BY-NC 4.0) "When I saw this tern so close by, I went into a panic that it had to be collected quickly because I'd have hated any wildlife to start scavenging on it and then land on our aviaries at home," she said. "That side of things really worries me." Louise McKay wants to protect her endangered glossy black cockatoo. (ABC South East SA: Liz Rymill) The couple said they had been satisfied with the reporting process, and were awaiting a follow-up call to confirm the case. "We took an extra step and contacted one of the senior ranger officers who assured us it would be dealt with quickly," Mrs McKay said. "The next time we approached the area, the bird had been removed." news.content_zh: 南澳内陆地区已检测到禽流感(H5N1),距罗布100多公里,这里一直是澳大利亚禽流感暴发的焦点。包括 Louise 和 Al McKay 在内的野生动物专家和鸟类饲养员正在敦促使用 疫苗 来保护濒危物种和私人鸟类。在石灰岩海岸和塔皮纳等内陆地区的凤头燕鸥中发现了这种病毒。南澳大利亚州政府正在制定一项国家战略,将 疫苗接种 用于优先圈养物种,例如仅在袋鼠岛上发现的极度濒危光泽黑色凤头鹦鹉。政府发言人指出,由于需要多次剂量,向自由生活的物种提供 疫苗 很困难。麦凯夫妇已实施生物安全措施,包括修改围栏和监测 野生鸟类,并正在等待案件确认。他们强调采取积极措施保护鸟类的重要性,因为它们很难重新安置并且需要特定的条件。该病毒正在大范围传播,鼓励社区报告潜在病例并对病禽保持警惕。

Agriculture Minister Julie Collins confirmed that the vaccination drive will initially focus on vulnerable priority species held in captivity. The announcement follows Australia's first reported mass death among seabirds, after the virus spread from migratory birds to local native species. Roughly 45 per cent of Australia's 850 bird species are endemic, leaving much of the country's unique wildlife acutely at risk. news.title: Australia: Bird Flu Detection in Wild Birds Doubles in Less Than 4 Days - Avian Flu Diary
news.rss_summary_html: Australia: Bird Flu Detection in Wild Birds Doubles in Less Than 4 Days  Avian Flu Diary
news.excerpt_original: Australia: Bird Flu Detection in Wild Birds Doubles in Less Than 4 Days Avian Flu Diary

news.content_title: Avian Flu Diary
news.content: Avian Flu Diary Covering Pandemic and Seasonal Flu, Emerging Infectious Diseases, public health, community & Individual preparedness. NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Thursday, August 13, 2026 Australia Changes How They Report H5N1 - Tasmania Detects 1st H5 Positive Bird Credit https://www.agriculture.gov.au/campaigns/birdflu #19,291 As we discussed a month ago, the number of daily citizen reports of sick or dead birds in Australia was already far outpacing their government's ability to investigate and test carcasses. Graphic generated by Gemini Yesterday, DAFF announced major changes in how they will report H5N1. No longer will individual detections be announced, instead they will track individual `events'. Event reporting *From 12 August 2026, we have changed how we report on H5 bird flu detections. Reporting will be based on events, rather than individual bird detections, where an event may involve one or more birds. The new number of positive events captures all previously reported individual confirmed detections. As of 4pm AEST, 13 August 2026, Australia has 186 confirmed events of H5 bird flu in wild birds. 10 in Western Australia (WA) 123 in South Australia (SA) 4 in New South Wales (NSW) 1 in Queensland (QLD) 48 in Victoria (VIC). As H5 bird flu is confirmed in more locations and species in Australia it will not be necessary to continue testing all species in known areas of transmission, or to test every bird involved in an investigation. Reporting will be targeted to provide a clear picture of the national H5 bird flu situation in wildlife in Australia and key developments. Definitions Investigation: An event where one or more wild birds or wild mammals showing signs of H5 bird flu have been reported to state or territory authorities and samples have been collected for laboratory testing. Positive event: An investigation where H5 bird flu has been confirmed through laboratory testing. Negative event: An investigation where laboratory testing has ruled out H5 bird flu. Hotline report: A report to relevant state or territory authorities through the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline or other official sources. Disclaimer Data reflects information provided by state and territory governments to the Australian Government as at 17:00 AEST daily. The Australian Government publishes this information for national reporting purposes. Responsibility for the accuracy, completeness and currency of the data remains with the relevant state or territory government. Due to differences in reporting timing, information on the national dashboard may differ from information published on state or territory government websites. While it is always disappointing to get less precise data, with the number of citizen reports (n=18,869) now running 13 times higher than the number of completed investigations (n=1459), something had to give. It isn't clear how this change will affect individual state and territorial reporting, as this new format hasn't yet appeared on either the Victoria or South Australia bird flu update web pages. Meanwhile, Tasmania has reported its first local positive detection of H5 in a brown skua. Samples have been sent to CSIRO for confirmation and subtyping. This from NRE Tas. H5 bird flu detected in Tasmania The Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania (NRE Tas) has detected H5 avian influenza (bird flu) in a wild brown skua. The bird was identified through NRE Tas surveillance efforts near Rocky Cape in the state’s north west and sent for testing at the Animal Health Laboratory in Launceston. Following the initial positive test result, samples have been sent to the CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness in Geelong to confirm the positive detection. This is Tasmania’s first positive detection in a wild bird. There have been no detections in poultry and there is no evidence of other species mortalities at this time. Tasmania has been preparing for the arrival of H5 bird flu, working with other government agencies, stakeholders and the community, and is well prepared to respond. NRE Tas will expand planned surveillance in and around the detection area, including King and Flinders islands. This will include further wildlife monitoring, sample collection and risk assessment activities. Tasmania has a robust biosecurity system but it is not possible to stop infected wildlife from entering Tasmania. The Tasmanian Avian Influenza Readiness and Response Plan sets out how NRE Tas will respond to an outbreak of H5 bird flu, and how you can prepare. In the event of an outbreak, our response will also be guided by the Animal Health Australia AUSVETPLAN response strategy for avian influenza. AUSVETPLAN contains the nationally agreed approach for responding to emergency animal disease incidents in Australia. Tasmania is also actively advancing vaccination for captive Orange-bellied Parrots as an additional protection measure for this endangered species however vaccination is not practical for most wild bird populations. There is no approved vaccine in Australia for backyard, domestic or commercial poultry and birds. There is also no vaccine available for seals, dolphins and Tasmanian devils. The Australian Government is working to make new vaccines available and ensure they are safe for use. For now, H5N1 has not been detected in poultry, livestock, or non-avian wildlife. But the odds that status quo will last are slim. Hopefully Australia is working on new and better ways to effectively communicate this rapidly evolving crisis to its public, and the world. A little over 2 weeks ago we looked at a preprint by Raina MacIntyre et al. (HPAI H5N1 risk in Australia: a model for the prediction of poultry outbreaks) which included a map showing current HPAI H5 detections overlaying poultry production zones. You can still view an updated interactive map at EPIWATCH, which shows the continued encroachment of HPAI in wild birds to these sensitive regions. Wednesday, August 12, 2026 J. Virology: Risk assessment of avian influenza A(H5N5) virus from the first human case using the ferret model Credit: Multiple transatlantic incursions of HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b A(H5N5) virus into North America and spillover to mammals #19,290 Last November we saw the first, and as far as we know - only - human infection with emerging H5N5 subtype of avian flu in a resident of Washington State who had contact with backyard poultry and/or wild birds. We've been following HPAI H5N5's spread in birds and small mammals - first in Europe, then in Canada and the United States - for several years, including a report last month; Preprint: HPAI H5N5 in a Polar Bear and Atlantic Walrus, Svalbard, 2026, with Widespread Seroconversion in Polar Bears. In late July we saw a Preprint: A lethal human H5N5 influenza virus isolate exhibits low pandemic risk traits, which somewhat reassuringly found the virus displayed relatively low pandemic risk traits: It replicated relatively poorly (compared to seasonal H1N1) in upper respiratory cell cultures, It has a more avian-like pH inactivation point (about 5.5) compared to human-adapted flu strains And - unlike in the Erdelyan et al. study (which reported rapid 100% mortality and some transmission in ferrets) - they reported that infected ferrets did not infect healthy co-housed ferrets. Today we've a study published in the Journal of Virology by researchers at the CDC's Influenza Division, NCIRD, which is slightly less reassuring. While they still found no evidence of airborne transmission in the ferret model, they report limited direct-contact transmission in 2 of 3 co-housed ferrets. And while the preprint reported moderate disease severity in ferrets, today's study reports uniformly severe/fatal disease, with rapid systemic spread. And where the preprint characterized WA/2148 as having reduced replication in human bronchial epithelial cultures, the CDC study instead found robust replication in polarized Calu-3 airway cells at both 33°C and 37°C. There were differences in both the methods and materials used in these two studies, which could account for these disparities. Today's study even notes that primary human airway cultures or organoids would provide a more physiologically relevant comparison than the proxies used by these two studies. And as always, the caveat remains that we can only draw limited conclusions from the evaluation and characterization of a single isolate, since even minor differences between strains or genotypes can make significant changes to its behavior. Due to it length, and technical nature, I've only reproduced the abstract and some excerpts from the study below. Follow the link to read it in its entirety. I'll have a brief postscript after you return. Risk assessment of avian influenza A(H5N5) virus from the first human case using the ferret model Authors: Joanna Pulit-Penaloza , Jessica A. Belser, Nicole Brock, Troy J. Kieran, Claudia Pappas, Hui Zeng, Xiangjie Sun, Juan A. De La Cruz, Yasuko Hatta, Han Di, C. Todd Davis , Taronna R. news.content_original: Avian Flu Diary Covering Pandemic and Seasonal Flu, Emerging Infectious Diseases, public health, community & Individual preparedness. NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Thursday, August 13, 2026 Australia Changes How They Report H5N1 - Tasmania Detects 1st H5 Positive Bird Credit https://www.agriculture.gov.au/campaigns/birdflu #19,291 As we discussed a month ago, the number of daily citizen reports of sick or dead birds in Australia was already far outpacing their government's ability to investigate and test carcasses. Graphic generated by Gemini Yesterday, DAFF announced major changes in how they will report H5N1. No longer will individual detections be announced, instead they will track individual `events'. Event reporting *From 12 August 2026, we have changed how we report on H5 bird flu detections. Reporting will be based on events, rather than individual bird detections, where an event may involve one or more birds. The new number of positive events captures all previously reported individual confirmed detections. As of 4pm AEST, 13 August 2026, Australia has 186 confirmed events of H5 bird flu in wild birds. 10 in Western Australia (WA) 123 in South Australia (SA) 4 in New South Wales (NSW) 1 in Queensland (QLD) 48 in Victoria (VIC). As H5 bird flu is confirmed in more locations and species in Australia it will not be necessary to continue testing all species in known areas of transmission, or to test every bird involved in an investigation. Reporting will be targeted to provide a clear picture of the national H5 bird flu situation in wildlife in Australia and key developments. Definitions Investigation: An event where one or more wild birds or wild mammals showing signs of H5 bird flu have been reported to state or territory authorities and samples have been collected for laboratory testing. Positive event: An investigation where H5 bird flu has been confirmed through laboratory testing. Negative event: An investigation where laboratory testing has ruled out H5 bird flu. Hotline report: A report to relevant state or territory authorities through the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline or other official sources. Disclaimer Data reflects information provided by state and territory governments to the Australian Government as at 17:00 AEST daily. The Australian Government publishes this information for national reporting purposes. Responsibility for the accuracy, completeness and currency of the data remains with the relevant state or territory government. Due to differences in reporting timing, information on the national dashboard may differ from information published on state or territory government websites. While it is always disappointing to get less precise data, with the number of citizen reports (n=18,869) now running 13 times higher than the number of completed investigations (n=1459), something had to give. It isn't clear how this change will affect individual state and territorial reporting, as this new format hasn't yet appeared on either the Victoria or South Australia bird flu update web pages. Meanwhile, Tasmania has reported its first local positive detection of H5 in a brown skua. Samples have been sent to CSIRO for confirmation and subtyping. This from NRE Tas. H5 bird flu detected in Tasmania The Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania (NRE Tas) has detected H5 avian influenza (bird flu) in a wild brown skua. The bird was identified through NRE Tas surveillance efforts near Rocky Cape in the state’s north west and sent for testing at the Animal Health Laboratory in Launceston. Following the initial positive test result, samples have been sent to the CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness in Geelong to confirm the positive detection. This is Tasmania’s first positive detection in a wild bird. There have been no detections in poultry and there is no evidence of other species mortalities at this time. Tasmania has been preparing for the arrival of H5 bird flu, working with other government agencies, stakeholders and the community, and is well prepared to respond. NRE Tas will expand planned surveillance in and around the detection area, including King and Flinders islands. This will include further wildlife monitoring, sample collection and risk assessment activities. Tasmania has a robust biosecurity system but it is not possible to stop infected wildlife from entering Tasmania. The Tasmanian Avian Influenza Readiness and Response Plan sets out how NRE Tas will respond to an outbreak of H5 bird flu, and how you can prepare. In the event of an outbreak, our response will also be guided by the Animal Health Australia AUSVETPLAN response strategy for avian influenza. AUSVETPLAN contains the nationally agreed approach for responding to emergency animal disease incidents in Australia. Tasmania is also actively advancing vaccination for captive Orange-bellied Parrots as an additional protection measure for this endangered species however vaccination is not practical for most wild bird populations. There is no approved vaccine in Australia for backyard, domestic or commercial poultry and birds. There is also no vaccine available for seals, dolphins and Tasmanian devils. The Australian Government is working to make new vaccines available and ensure they are safe for use. For now, H5N1 has not been detected in poultry, livestock, or non-avian wildlife. But the odds that status quo will last are slim. Hopefully Australia is working on new and better ways to effectively communicate this rapidly evolving crisis to its public, and the world. A little over 2 weeks ago we looked at a preprint by Raina MacIntyre et al. (HPAI H5N1 risk in Australia: a model for the prediction of poultry outbreaks) which included a map showing current HPAI H5 detections overlaying poultry production zones. You can still view an updated interactive map at EPIWATCH, which shows the continued encroachment of HPAI in wild birds to these sensitive regions. Wednesday, August 12, 2026 J. Virology: Risk assessment of avian influenza A(H5N5) virus from the first human case using the ferret model Credit: Multiple transatlantic incursions of HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b A(H5N5) virus into North America and spillover to mammals #19,290 Last November we saw the first, and as far as we know - only - human infection with emerging H5N5 subtype of avian flu in a resident of Washington State who had contact with backyard poultry and/or wild birds. We've been following HPAI H5N5's spread in birds and small mammals - first in Europe, then in Canada and the United States - for several years, including a report last month; Preprint: HPAI H5N5 in a Polar Bear and Atlantic Walrus, Svalbard, 2026, with Widespread Seroconversion in Polar Bears. In late July we saw a Preprint: A lethal human H5N5 influenza virus isolate exhibits low pandemic risk traits, which somewhat reassuringly found the virus displayed relatively low pandemic risk traits: It replicated relatively poorly (compared to seasonal H1N1) in upper respiratory cell cultures, It has a more avian-like pH inactivation point (about 5.5) compared to human-adapted flu strains And - unlike in the Erdelyan et al. study (which reported rapid 100% mortality and some transmission in ferrets) - they reported that infected ferrets did not infect healthy co-housed ferrets. Today we've a study published in the Journal of Virology by researchers at the CDC's Influenza Division, NCIRD, which is slightly less reassuring. While they still found no evidence of airborne transmission in the ferret model, they report limited direct-contact transmission in 2 of 3 co-housed ferrets. And while the preprint reported moderate disease severity in ferrets, today's study reports uniformly severe/fatal disease, with rapid systemic spread. And where the preprint characterized WA/2148 as having reduced replication in human bronchial epithelial cultures, the CDC study instead found robust replication in polarized Calu-3 airway cells at both 33°C and 37°C. There were differences in both the methods and materials used in these two studies, which could account for these disparities. Today's study even notes that primary human airway cultures or organoids would provide a more physiologically relevant comparison than the proxies used by these two studies. And as always, the caveat remains that we can only draw limited conclusions from the evaluation and characterization of a single isolate, since even minor differences between strains or genotypes can make significant changes to its behavior. Due to it length, and technical nature, I've only reproduced the abstract and some excerpts from the study below. Follow the link to read it in its entirety. analysis.location_and_population: Australia (national), with confirmed events in Western Australia (10), South Australia (123), New South Wales (4), Queensland (1), Victoria (48), and Tasmania (first local detection in a wild brown skua).
analysis.event: Australia’s Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) changed its reporting method for H5 avian influenza in wild birds from individual detections to aggregated ‘events’ starting 12 August 2026. Tasmania reported its first local H5-positive wild bird (brown skua) on 13 August 2026.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: As of 13 August 2026, 186 confirmed H5 bird flu events in wild birds nationwide. No detections in poultry, livestock, or non-avian wildlife reported. Risk assessment notes rapid expansion of H5 detections in wild birds and potential future incursions into sensitive poultry zones.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: DAFF now reports aggregated ‘events’ rather than individual detections to manage high caseload; Tasmania expanded surveillance around the detection area and is preparing response plans under AUSVETPLAN. No approved vaccines exist for poultry or most wild species in Australia; CSIRO confirmation and subtyping of the Tasmanian sample are pending. Data reflect state/territory submissions to DAFF; discrepancies may occur across jurisdictions.

analysis.brief_en: On 12 August 2026, Australia’s Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry shifted its H5 avian influenza reporting from individual bird detections to aggregated ‘events’ to manage a surge in wild-bird cases. By 13 August, 186 confirmed H5 events were recorded across six states and territories, with Tasmania reporting its first local positive in a wild brown skua. No poultry or livestock detections have been reported, but authorities warn that incursions into sensitive poultry zones are increasingly likely. Tasmania is expanding wildlife surveillance and preparing response measures under the national AUSVETPLAN framework, while CSIRO conducts confirmatory testing. Vaccines remain unavailable for most wild species and poultry in Australia.

analysis_en.time: Event date: 12–13 August 2026 (reporting window). Publication date: 8 August 2026 (Avian Flu Diary post date).
analysis_en.location_and_population: Australia (national), with confirmed events in Western Australia (10), South Australia (123), New South Wales (4), Queensland (1), Victoria (48), and Tasmania (first local detection in a wild brown skua).
analysis_en.event: Australia’s Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) changed its reporting method for H5 avian influenza in wild birds from individual detections to aggregated ‘events’ starting 12 August 2026. Tasmania reported its first local H5-positive wild bird (brown skua) on 13 August 2026.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: As of 13 August 2026, 186 confirmed H5 bird flu events in wild birds nationwide. No detections in poultry, livestock, or non-avian wildlife reported. Risk assessment notes rapid expansion of H5 detections in wild birds and potential future incursions into sensitive poultry zones.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: DAFF now reports aggregated ‘events’ rather than individual detections to manage high caseload; Tasmania expanded surveillance around the detection area and is preparing response plans under AUSVETPLAN. No approved vaccines exist for poultry or most wild species in Australia; CSIRO confirmation and subtyping of the Tasmanian sample are pending. Data reflect state/territory submissions to DAFF; discrepancies may occur across jurisdictions.

news.title_zh: 澳大利亚:野生鸟类 禽流感检测量在不到 4 天内翻倍 - 禽流感日记
news.source_body_en: On 12 August 2026, Australia’s Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry shifted its H5 avian influenza reporting from individual bird detections to aggregated ‘events’ to manage a surge in wild-bird cases. By 13 August, 186 confirmed H5 events were recorded across six states and territories, with Tasmania reporting its first local positive in a wild brown skua. No poultry or livestock detections have been reported, but authorities warn that incursions into sensitive poultry zones are increasingly likely. Tasmania is expanding wildlife surveillance and preparing response measures under the national AUSVETPLAN framework, while CSIRO conducts confirmatory testing. Vaccines remain unavailable for most wild species and poultry in Australia.

analysis.brief_en: Tasmania has confirmed its first case of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) in poultry, according to ABC News on 12 August 2026. The detection marks the state’s initial H5N1 finding and has prompted concern within the local poultry sector, with farmers described as 'very nervous' and a scheduled poultry show cancelled. Authorities are investigating the extent of the outbreak, which has been detected in a second location in Tasmania. No human infections have been reported in the available evidence. The event underscores heightened biosecurity risks for Australia’s poultry industry and ongoing surveillance efforts.

Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search Support Menu Cambodia confirms human H5N1 avian flu case as H5N1 hits more Utah egg farms News brief July 16, 2026 Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Share mswine / Flickr cc Earlier this week Cambodian officials announced the country’s fifth human H5N1 avian flu case this year, this one involving a 9-month-old girl. The girl has been hospitalized and is receiving intensive care. So far no source of infection or exposure has been found, but the child’s close contacts are being given oseltamivir (Tamiflu) as a precaution. Cambodia reported 19 human cases of H5N1 in 2025, eight of which were fatal. Most recent cases in Cambodia have involved a reassortant (2.3.2.1e) between an older H5N1 clade that has circulated in Cambodia since 2014 and the newer clade 2.3.4.4b virus that is circulating globally. Utah reports H5N1 in poultry, cattle In US news, the US Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) reported for the second week in a row an egg farm H5N1 outbreak in Cache County, Utah, affecting 275,100 birds. In the past 30 days, 1.49 million birds have been hit with H5N1 in the United States. APHIS also noted several new detections of avian flu in cattle in Utah and Idaho, with each state reporting four confirmed cases this week. Twenty-six cattle in the past 30 days have been confirmed to be infected with H5N1, raising the year’s total to 81 cases. Moms who receive COVID, flu vaccines during pregnancy more likely to vaccinate their babies, study says News brief July 16, 2026 Meghan Holohan Topics Childhood Vaccines COVID-19 Influenza Vaccines Adult (non-flu) Vaccines Pressmaster / iStock Infants born to mothers vaccinated before, during, or soon after pregnancy for COVID-19 or flu were more likely to receive vaccines than those born to unvaccinated mothers, suggests a study published in Pediatrics. “The results show that maternal vaccination is strongly associated with infant vaccination in the first year of life, especially when vaccination occurred during pregnancy or shortly after delivery,” wrote the study’s authors, from Kaiser Permanente Northern California. “Improving maternal vaccine coverage during those times may improve child vaccine coverage, ensuring continuous protection in early life.” Implications for policymaking, intervention development The researchers looked at 82,533 mother-infant pairs in a retrospective cohort study of babies born from August 18, 2021, to March 31, 2024, to see how mothers’ vaccination status affected their babies’ likelihood of receiving flu or COVID-19 vaccines. The mothers of 32,370 babies (39% of the total) received a COVID-19 vaccine during pregnancy, and 43,806 babies (53%) were born to mothers who received a flu shot while pregnant. Improving maternal vaccine coverage during those times may improve child vaccine coverage, ensuring continuous protection in early life. If moms received a COVID-19 vaccine during pregnancy, their babies were 9.65 times more likely to also receive the COVID-19 vaccine. Moms who received a flu shot had babies who were 3.67 times more likely to also receive one. Babies had a 66.2% probability of getting a flu shot and a 23.4% chance of getting a COVID vaccine before they turned 1 year. “Our findings also suggest that some women may not be comfortable being vaccinated during pregnancy but are willing to vaccinate their infants; differences in attitudes toward vaccinating themselves vs their children have been observed in qualitative studies of parents, although not specifically around pregnancy,” the authors wrote. “Future studies examining the interplay of these factors will be an important part of making policy and developing interventions.” Most measles patients who sought care at Prisma Health in South Carolina were kids News brief July 16, 2026 Sarah Boden Topics Measles Most of the measles patients Prisma Health Greenville Memorial Hospital cared for during South Carolina's recent outbreak were kids aged 10 years or younger. NIH According to a letter from the health system's physicians, published yesterday in the New England Journal of Medicine, Prisma treated 81 people for measles from October 2025 to April 2026. A total of 997 cases were reported to the South Carolina Department of Public Health during the outbreak. The cases were concentrated in the Upstate region, particularly Spartanburg County, where measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination coverage was 88.9%. The letter notes that at least 73% of those who sought care at Prisma were unvaccinated. Statewide, 93% of cases were among unvaccinated South Carolinians. The most common symptoms observed by Prisma clinicians were fever, cough or other respiratory symptoms, and the characteristic rash of flat red spots. Koplik spots, which are tiny, bluish-white clustered lesions on the inside of the mouth, were reported in a quarter of patients. Severe outcomes, lasting complications None of the 81 patients seen at Prisma Health died. Ten children and three adults were hospitalized, primarily for dehydration, respiratory problems, or pneumonia. Most hospitalized patients were sent home within 72 hours, though the report notes that two had prolonged hospitalizations due to measles encephalitis, a life-threatening inflammation of the brain. One of the two was discharged to an inpatient rehabilitation facility and "as of the time of this report is receiving ongoing outpatient therapy." The other patient recovered but continues to have headaches and a vocal tic. Within a month after being diagnosed with measles, 24 of the patients had concurrent or subsequent infections. The most common infections were pneumonia, a type of ear infection called otitis media, and sinusitis, an inflammation of the sinus tissue. Utah reports H5N1 in poultry, cattle In US news, the US Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) reported for the second week in a row an egg farm H5N1 outbreak in Cache County, Utah, affecting 275,100 birds. In the past 30 days, 1.49 million birds have been hit with H5N1 in the United States. APHIS also noted several new detections of avian flu in cattle in Utah and Idaho, with each state reporting four confirmed cases this week. Twenty-six cattle in the past 30 days have been confirmed to be infected with H5N1, raising the year’s total to 81 cases. Moms who receive COVID, flu vaccines during pregnancy more likely to vaccinate their babies, study says News brief July 16, 2026 Meghan Holohan Topics Childhood Vaccines COVID-19 Influenza Vaccines Adult (non-flu) Vaccines Pressmaster / iStock Infants born to mothers vaccinated before, during, or soon after pregnancy for COVID-19 or flu were more likely to receive vaccines than those born to unvaccinated mothers, suggests a study published in Pediatrics. “The results show that maternal vaccination is strongly associated with infant vaccination in the first year of life, especially when vaccination occurred during pregnancy or shortly after delivery,” wrote the study’s authors, from Kaiser Permanente Northern California. “Improving maternal vaccine coverage during those times may improve child vaccine coverage, ensuring continuous protection in early life.” Implications for policymaking, intervention development The researchers looked at 82,533 mother-infant pairs in a retrospective cohort study of babies born from August 18, 2021, to March 31, 2024, to see how mothers’ vaccination status affected their babies’ likelihood of receiving flu or COVID-19 vaccines. The mothers of 32,370 babies (39% of the total) received a COVID-19 vaccine during pregnancy, and 43,806 babies (53%) were born to mothers who received a flu shot while pregnant. Improving maternal vaccine coverage during those times may improve child vaccine coverage, ensuring continuous protection in early life. If moms received a COVID-19 vaccine during pregnancy, their babies were 9.65 times more likely to also receive the COVID-19 vaccine. Moms who received a flu shot had babies who were 3.67 times more likely to also receive one. Babies had a 66.2% probability of getting a flu shot and a 23.4% chance of getting a COVID vaccine before they turned 1 year. “Our findings also suggest that some women may not be comfortable being vaccinated during pregnancy but are willing to vaccinate their infants; differences in attitudes toward vaccinating themselves vs their children have been observed in qualitative studies of parents, although not specifically around pregnancy,” the authors wrote. “Future studies examining the interplay of these factors will be an important part of making policy and developing interventions.” Most measles patients who sought care at Prisma Health in South Carolina were kids News brief July 16, 2026 Sarah Boden Topics Measles Most of the measles patients Prisma Health Greenville Memorial Hospital cared for during South Carolina's recent outbreak were kids aged 10 years or younger. NIH According to a letter from the health system's physicians, published yesterday in the New England Journal of Medicine, Prisma treated 81 people for measles from October 2025 to April 2026. A total of 997 cases were reported to the South Carolina Department of Public Health during the outbreak. The cases were concentrated in the Upstate region, particularly Spartanburg County, where measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination coverage was 88.9%. The letter notes that at least 73% of those who sought care at Prisma were unvaccinated. Statewide, 93% of cases were among unvaccinated South Carolinians. The most common symptoms observed by Prisma clinicians were fever, cough or other respiratory symptoms, and the characteristic rash of flat red spots. Koplik spots, which are tiny, bluish-white clustered lesions on the inside of the mouth, were reported in a quarter of patients. Severe outcomes, lasting complications None of the 81 patients seen at Prisma Health died. Ten children and three adults were hospitalized, primarily for dehydration, respiratory problems, or pneumonia. Most hospitalized patients were sent home within 72 hours, though the report notes that two had prolonged hospitalizations due to measles encephalitis, a life-threatening inflammation of the brain. One of the two was discharged to an inpatient rehabilitation facility and "as of the time of this report is receiving ongoing outpatient therapy." The other patient recovered but continues to have headaches and a vocal tic. Within a month after being diagnosed with measles, 24 of the patients had concurrent or subsequent infections. The most common infections were pneumonia, a type of ear infection called otitis media, and sinusitis, an inflammation of the sinus tissue. analysis.brief_en: Cambodia confirmed its fifth human H5N1 avian influenza case of 2026 on July 16, involving a 9-month-old girl who was hospitalized in intensive care; the source of infection remains unidentified and close contacts are receiving antiviral prophylaxis. In the United States, the USDA reported a second consecutive week of H5N1 outbreaks in Utah’s poultry sector, affecting 275,100 birds on an egg farm, while 1.49 million birds across the country have been impacted over the past 30 days. Utah and Idaho also reported new H5N1 detections in cattle, bringing the 2026 total to 81 confirmed cases, including 26 detected in the last month. The concurrent spread in animals raises concerns about zoonotic spillover risk, though no direct epidemiological link between the Cambodian human case and the US animal outbreaks has been established.

One expert expects the disease will spread across the continent within a year. Photograph: DEA/P. JACCOD/De Agostini/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Greater crested terns were the first native bird to suffer a mass mortality event from bird flu in Australia. One expert expects the disease will spread across the continent within a year. Photograph: DEA/P. JACCOD/De Agostini/Getty Images When bird flu hit the UK, suffering seabirds died in their thousands. Australia’s wild flocks will soon do the same Australia’s bird population will experience ‘large mortalities’ and risk species loss, modelling based on global outbreaks shows Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here Sandwich terns are a graceful seabird known for their committed, forceful and spectacular plunging dives into the ocean to catch fish. Thousands of the species started to fall sick across Europe in 2022 with tens of thousands dying as a lineage of the H5N1 bird flu – 2.3.4.4b – spread through the continent’s wild flocks. The effects of the virus on the brain cause the terns to flounder on the ground, craning and straining their necks in a suffering behaviour known as star-gazing. It is difficult to watch. “I remember a colony at Scolt Head Island in Norfolk,” says Prof James Pearce-Higgins, the director of science at the British Trust for Ornithology. “You had adult terns trying to mate with dead terns and chicks begging for food from their dying parents. View image in fullscreen The sandwich tern (pictured) is a close relative of the greater crested tern, which is common in Australia. Photograph: Natural England/Allan Drewitt/PA “It was a real sense of a colony collapse as you watched this transfer of the virus between birds.” Sandwich terns are close relatives of greater crested terns, which are seen all around Australia and were the first native bird to suffer a mass mortality event from the disease in Australia on South Australia’s Limestone Coast. Since the virus re-emerged in Europe in 2021 it has swept over every other continent, killing millions of birds and mammals, and infecting more than 400 bird species as well as mammals – in particular, seals and sea lions. The virus was finally detected in Australia two months ago in migratory seabirds that likely brought the disease from breeding grounds in the subantarctic. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter This week, the federal government revealed analysis of the potential threat to Australia’s wildlife which showed almost 400 species of birds and mammals were at “high risk” or worse if they caught the disease. One expert who worked on the analysis, Prof John Woinarski of Charles Darwin University, tells the Guardian he expects the disease will have spread across the continent within a year. The last continent: how deadly bird flu travelled the world before landing on a remote Australian beach Read more Pearce-Higgins says: “I would expect Australia is going to experience large mortalities, like those we have been through, and it’s going to put some species at risk.” Almost half of Australia’s bird species are unique to the continent, meaning that a lot of uncertainty comes with predicting what H5N1 could do to the animal population. It also means the risk of the virus causing planet-wide extinctions is higher now that every continent is affected. Death toll will be ‘confronting’ “We’ve been looking overseas since 2021 and seeing the advance of this virus,” says Dr Sara Ryding, an evolutionary ecologist at Deakin University. “It has been horrible overseas – tens of thousands of birds dying in single colonies. “The concern was, we knew it was going to arrive eventually – how could it not? But we didn’t know what it would look like when it got here.” View image in fullscreen Spending time around bodies of water, where the virus can live for months, can make animals susceptible to bird flu. Photograph: Danielle Connor/Alamy Ryding has led research to project the level of risk from H5N1 for all Australia’s bird families by developing a model based on official reports of the disease from around the globe to the World Organisation for Animal Health. The research suggested the most at-risk families of birds were gannets and boobies (Sulidae), followed in descending order of risk by cranes (Gruidae), darters (Anhingidae), ducks, geese and swans (Anatidae), and gulls, terns and noddies (Laridae). But a host of other bird families – including pelicans, crows, ravens, falcons and kestrels – were all predicted to be susceptible. While many species of those birds are not considered threatened, the sight of large numbers of dead and sick birds, particularly larger species like swans and pelicans, “is going to be confronting,” Ryding says. “I don’t want to cause panic, but we have seen the devastation it has caused overseas and there’s no reason to think it will be any less devastating here,” she says. “I think it will be really bad.” Studies have identified several behaviours that can make animals susceptible to catching the disease, such as scavenging dead and dying animals for food (as do gulls and Tasmanian devils), spending time in dense colonies (like seals and waterbirds) and spending time around bodies of water where the virus can live for weeks or months, or where other infected animals might also be around. ‘Devastating’ for seals and sea lions The virus has been particularly damaging for seals and sea lions. Tens of thousands of seals and sea lions have died in outbreaks in Peru, Chile, Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina and, most recently, on Australia’s subantarctic territory of Heard Island and McDonald Islands. The virus can cause debilitating conditions for the seals and sea lions – known collectively as pinnipeds – with severe neurological and respiratory symptoms. View image in fullscreen Australian fur seals near Maria Island, Tasmania. Because they live in dense groups, seals are particularly susceptible to bird flu. Photograph: Robert Wyatt/Alamy Australia has three resident pinniped species – the New Zealand fur seal, the Australian fur seal and the already endangered Australian sea lion – and government analysis has suggested the risk for all three from the virus is “very high”, meaning “very severe reduction in population size or viability is predicted” if the virus reaches them. Dr Saia Bartes is an Argentinian marine biologist who has just completed her PhD on Australian fur seals at Deakin University and has helped study declines in South American sea lions after the virus struck there. View image in fullscreen A young Australian fur seal near Montague Island, NSW. Seal numbers are still recovering from commercial hunting. Photograph: By Wildestanimal/Getty Images “It was devastating for them. In north Patagonia, we lost a third of the sea lions,” she says. Because pinnipeds often share space with infected birds, and tend to be in tightly packed groups, Bartes says they are particularly susceptible. Pinniped numbers are still recovering from commercial hunting, she says, and “they could start declining again really quickly, which is happening in South America” if the virus found them. Back in the UK, Pearce-Higgins says there is some hope. Their experience of collaboration with conservation groups, volunteers and local authorities through weekly and later monthly meetings had been critical in the response. And there were some signs the impacts of the virus may be slowing. “The hope is that because a lot of these birds are long-lived, the population could be more resilient. But we still don’t really know the probabilities of future outbreaks,” he says. “It might look really bad for a few years, but the hope is that [Australia] can focus on the conservation of what is left.” Explore more on these topics Bird flu Birds Wildlife Endangered species features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Massachusetts teen accused of killing mother and brother used ChatGPT US conducted ‘mass spying campaign’ against leftwing groups and anti-ICE protesters, records reveal Nigel Farage set for decisive but arguably empty victory in Clacton Donald Trump empowers US private companies to conduct cyber-attacks ‘Show the necessary respect’: German athlete Kolbe slams racist abuse of teammates More on this story More on this story Native birds in captivity to be vaccinated against H5 bird flu as Australia prepares for more mass mortalities Jean hoped bird flu wouldn’t come to Australia.
