JACCOD/De Agostini/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Greater crested terns were the first native bird to suffer a mass mortality event from bird flu in Australia. One expert expects the disease will spread across the continent within a year. Photograph: DEA/P. JACCOD/De Agostini/Getty Images When bird flu hit the UK, suffering seabirds died in their thousands. Australia’s wild flocks will soon do the same Australia’s bird population will experience ‘large mortalities’ and risk species loss, modelling based on global outbreaks shows Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here Sandwich terns are a graceful seabird known for their committed, forceful and spectacular plunging dives into the ocean to catch fish. Thousands of the species started to fall sick across Europe in 2022 with tens of thousands dying as a lineage of the H5N1 bird flu – 2.3.4.4b – spread through the continent’s wild flocks. The effects of the virus on the brain cause the terns to flounder on the ground, craning and straining their necks in a suffering behaviour known as star-gazing. It is difficult to watch. “I remember a colony at Scolt Head Island in Norfolk,” says Prof James Pearce-Higgins, the director of science at the British Trust for Ornithology. “You had adult terns trying to mate with dead terns and chicks begging for food from their dying parents. View image in fullscreen The sandwich tern (pictured) is a close relative of the greater crested tern, which is common in Australia. Photograph: Natural England/Allan Drewitt/PA “It was a real sense of a colony collapse as you watched this transfer of the virus between birds.” Sandwich terns are close relatives of greater crested terns, which are seen all around Australia and were the first native bird to suffer a mass mortality event from the disease in Australia on South Australia’s Limestone Coast. Since the virus re-emerged in Europe in 2021 it has swept over every other continent, killing millions of birds and mammals, and infecting more than 400 bird species as well as mammals – in particular, seals and sea lions. The virus was finally detected in Australia two months ago in migratory seabirds that likely brought the disease from breeding grounds in the subantarctic. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter This week, the federal government revealed analysis of the potential threat to Australia’s wildlife which showed almost 400 species of birds and mammals were at “high risk” or worse if they caught the disease. One expert who worked on the analysis, Prof John Woinarski of Charles Darwin University, tells the Guardian he expects the disease will have spread across the continent within a year. The last continent: how deadly bird flu travelled the world before landing on a remote Australian beach Read more Pearce-Higgins says: “I would expect Australia is going to experience large mortalities, like those we have been through, and it’s going to put some species at risk.” Almost half of Australia’s bird species are unique to the continent, meaning that a lot of uncertainty comes with predicting what H5N1 could do to the animal population. It also means the risk of the virus causing planet-wide extinctions is higher now that every continent is affected. Death toll will be ‘confronting’ “We’ve been looking overseas since 2021 and seeing the advance of this virus,” says Dr Sara Ryding, an evolutionary ecologist at Deakin University. “It has been horrible overseas – tens of thousands of birds dying in single colonies. “The concern was, we knew it was going to arrive eventually – how could it not? But we didn’t know what it would look like when it got here.” View image in fullscreen Spending time around bodies of water, where the virus can live for months, can make animals susceptible to bird flu. Photograph: Danielle Connor/Alamy Ryding has led research to project the level of risk from H5N1 for all Australia’s bird families by developing a model based on official reports of the disease from around the globe to the World Organisation for Animal Health. The research suggested the most at-risk families of birds were gannets and boobies (Sulidae), followed in descending order of risk by cranes (Gruidae), darters (Anhingidae), ducks, geese and swans (Anatidae), and gulls, terns and noddies (Laridae). But a host of other bird families – including pelicans, crows, ravens, falcons and kestrels – were all predicted to be susceptible. While many species of those birds are not considered threatened, the sight of large numbers of dead and sick birds, particularly larger species like swans and pelicans, “is going to be confronting,” Ryding says. “I don’t want to cause panic, but we have seen the devastation it has caused overseas and there’s no reason to think it will be any less devastating here,” she says. “I think it will be really bad.” Studies have identified several behaviours that can make animals susceptible to catching the disease, such as scavenging dead and dying animals for food (as do gulls and Tasmanian devils), spending time in dense colonies (like seals and waterbirds) and spending time around bodies of water where the virus can live for weeks or months, or where other infected animals might also be around. ‘Devastating’ for seals and sea lions The virus has been particularly damaging for seals and sea lions. Tens of thousands of seals and sea lions have died in outbreaks in Peru, Chile, Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina and, most recently, on Australia’s subantarctic territory of Heard Island and McDonald Islands. The virus can cause debilitating conditions for the seals and sea lions – known collectively as pinnipeds – with severe neurological and respiratory symptoms. View image in fullscreen Australian fur seals near Maria Island, Tasmania. Because they live in dense groups, seals are particularly susceptible to bird flu. Photograph: Robert Wyatt/Alamy Australia has three resident pinniped species – the New Zealand fur seal, the Australian fur seal and the already endangered Australian sea lion – and government analysis has suggested the risk for all three from the virus is “very high”, meaning “very severe reduction in population size or viability is predicted” if the virus reaches them. Dr Saia Bartes is an Argentinian marine biologist who has just completed her PhD on Australian fur seals at Deakin University and has helped study declines in South American sea lions after the virus struck there. View image in fullscreen A young Australian fur seal near Montague Island, NSW. Seal numbers are still recovering from commercial hunting. Photograph: By Wildestanimal/Getty Images “It was devastating for them. In north Patagonia, we lost a third of the sea lions,” she says. Because pinnipeds often share space with infected birds, and tend to be in tightly packed groups, Bartes says they are particularly susceptible. Pinniped numbers are still recovering from commercial hunting, she says, and “they could start declining again really quickly, which is happening in South America” if the virus found them. Back in the UK, Pearce-Higgins says there is some hope. Their experience of collaboration with conservation groups, volunteers and local authorities through weekly and later monthly meetings had been critical in the response. And there were some signs the impacts of the virus may be slowing. “The hope is that because a lot of these birds are long-lived, the population could be more resilient. But we still don’t really know the probabilities of future outbreaks,” he says. “It might look really bad for a few years, but the hope is that [Australia] can focus on the conservation of what is left.” Explore more on these topics Bird flu Birds Wildlife Endangered species features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Massachusetts teen accused of killing mother and brother used ChatGPT US conducted ‘mass spying campaign’ against leftwing groups and anti-ICE protesters, records reveal Nigel Farage set for decisive but arguably empty victory in Clacton Donald Trump empowers US private companies to conduct cyber-attacks ‘Show the necessary respect’: German athlete Kolbe slams racist abuse of teammates More on this story More on this story Native birds in captivity to be vaccinated against H5 bird flu as Australia prepares for more mass mortalities Jean hoped bird flu wouldn’t come to Australia. analysis.time: Published 2026-08-08; event timeline spans 2021–2026 with current risk projection within one year from expert statements.
analysis.location_and_population: Australia (continent-wide), South Australia’s Limestone Coast (first mass mortality event), Norfolk UK (historical reference), subantarctic breeding grounds (source of introduction). Affected populations include wild seabirds (greater crested terns, sandwich terns, gannets, boobies, cranes, darters, ducks, geese, swans, gulls, terns, noddies, pelicans, crows, ravens, falcons, kestrels), pinnipeds (seals and sea lions), and unique Australian bird species.
analysis.event: Reported mass mortality events and projected large-scale die-offs of wild birds and marine mammals in Australia due to highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) lineage 2.3.4.4b, with confirmed first native bird mass mortality event in Australia and federal government risk analysis indicating high-risk species. The report synthesizes expert modelling and official assessments.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Tens of thousands of seabirds died in single European colonies since 2022; millions of birds and mammals killed globally since 2021; over 400 bird species and multiple mammal species infected; Australian federal analysis identifies almost 400 bird and mammal species at high risk or worse; pinniped species (New Zealand fur seal, Australian fur seal, Australian sea lion) at very high risk; projected continent-wide spread within one year; risk of species loss and planet-wide extinctions heightened by global spread.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Australia detected H5N1 two months prior in migratory seabirds; federal government revealed analysis of potential threat; expert modelling based on global outbreaks to WOAH; research identifies high-risk bird families; uncertainty remains about exact impact on unique Australian species; no reported human cases in Australia in the evidence; prevention measures implied through surveillance and risk modelling.

analysis.brief_en: Australia faces imminent large-scale die-offs of wild birds and marine mammals from highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) lineage 2.3.4.4b, according to modelling and federal risk assessments. The first confirmed mass mortality event in native Australian birds occurred on South Australia’s Limestone Coast, with greater crested terns affected. Experts warn the virus will likely spread continent-wide within a year, mirroring devastation seen in Europe since 2022 where tens of thousands of seabirds perished in single colonies. Nearly 400 Australian bird and mammal species are judged at high risk, including iconic pinnipeds such as the endangered Australian sea lion and Australian fur seal, for which the risk is classified as very high. While no human cases are reported in the evidence, researchers caution that the continent’s unique bird fauna face uncertain outcomes, raising concerns about species loss and elevated global extinction risks as the virus now circulates on every continent.

news.content_zh: 根据建模和联邦风险评估,澳大利亚面临着 野生鸟类 和 高致病性禽流感 A(H5N1) 谱系 2.3.4.4b 海洋哺乳动物即将大规模灭绝。首次确认的澳大利亚本土鸟类大规模 死亡率 事件发生在南澳大利亚的石灰岩海岸,受影响的是更大的凤头燕鸥。专家警告说,这种病毒可能会在一年内在整个欧洲大陆传播,这与 2022 年以来欧洲所遭受的破坏如出一辙,当时数以万计的海鸟在单个栖息地死亡。近 400 种澳大利亚鸟类和哺乳动物物种被判定为高风险,其中包括标志性鳍足类动物,如濒临灭绝的澳大利亚海狮和澳大利亚毛皮海豹,其风险被归类为极高。虽然证据中没有报告人类病例,但研究人员警告说,非洲大陆独特的鸟类动物群面临着不确定的结果,随着病毒现在在各大洲传播,引发了人们对物种丧失和全球灭绝风险升高的担忧。

news.content_title: H5N1 sparks a very Australian epidemic
news.content: H5N1 bird flu has reached Australia's shores and is threatening to infect some of the country's most unique wildlife. Australasia is the last continent to be hit by the highly infectious avian influenza H5N1 , a new strain of which has been circulating worldwide since 2020. Since recording its first case in June, more than 200 wild seabirds in Australia have been infected, with fears that the highly infectious flu could quickly 'jump' to other species. While H5N1 has infected animals from foxes to sea lions in other parts of the world in recent years, the epidemic now threatens some of Australia's most iconic wildlife – many of which are found nowhere else on earth. An Australian government assessment of more than 2,000 native species warned that nearly one in five faces a high risk from the deadly H5N1 bird flu, with hundreds of unique birds and mammals vulnerable to severe population reductions or even extinction. Those animals include iconic species like the Tasmanian devils, quolls, and dingoes. Other aquatic mammals, including the platypus, which is only found in Australia, are at risk of infection through contact with bird droppings in shared wetlands and coastal environments. Tasmanian devils are an endangered species - HANDOUT/Aussie Ark/AFP via Getty Images Dingoes are among the mammals that are unique to Australia - iStockphoto "This could be quite devastating to what is a unique ecosystem with endangered populations," Professor Ian Brown, Head of Avian Virology at The Pirbright Institute, told The Telegraph. "It's been a waiting game [...] I don't think that any are that surprised that the virus has got to Australia now," Prof Ashley C. Banyard, an avian virology expert at the government's Animal and Plant Health Agency, said. "I think people have been expecting it [the virus] to reach Australia as several bird species that travel to that region have long-distance migratory pathways from areas where the virus has been detected previously, and we continue to detect positives on British Overseas Territories in the sub-Antarctic region where these species migrate from", said Prof Banyard. The government is set to begin a vaccination campaign in the coming weeks to protect some of these endangered species that are conserved in captivity – beginning with rare birds like the orange-bellied parrot, the regent honeyeater, and Western Australia's black cockatoos. "We've been very clear that we cannot stop the H5 bird flu from spreading amongst wild birds, but we can take action to protect the species most at risk, and the vaccination is now part of that response," Australia's Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said in a statement on Tuesday. "Obviously, Australia wants to protect these species; they're of high conservation concern, and they want to avoid this virus ripping through them," said Prof Banyard. "But I think the bigger picture is how do you deal with the introductions from wild birds, which we've all suffered with for many years across Europe and elsewhere. "Ultimately biosecurity is essential to prevention in poultry species and with wild bird cases increasing in the region, stringent biosecurity will be critical in preventing this becoming an even bigger problem," he added. Since 2022, H5N1 has spread at a rapid pace across the world, decimating millions of domestic and wild bird populations as well as infecting a wide range of animals, from otters to seals to lions, tigers, and bears. It has had a huge impact on the farming industry and sent the price of eggs and poultry meat soaring as flocks are culled to try to contain the spread of the virus. In Britain and the EU, almost 48 million birds were culled between 2021 and 2022 alone at the height of the bird-flu season. This risk now threatens the Australian poultry industry, which contributes roughly $4.1 billion to the regional agricultural industry every year. "It hasn't hit poultry [in Australia] yet. If it does get into flocks, it's always going to be problematic. But I would imagine flocks in Australia and New Zealand are quite spread apart, and so the risk of lateral spread is probably lower [than in the UK]," said Prof Banyard. The virus also poses a threat to human health, and it has long been feared that H5N1 could spark the next pandemic, should it develop the ability to spread between people. More than 1,000 people have contracted the virus since it first emerged in the late 1990s, mostly through close contact with sickened animals, almost half of whom have died. Australian authorities currently deem the risk to human health as "low", and have invested $113 million Australian dollars (£59 million) into preparedness activities, including boosting national stockpiles of pandemic flu vaccines, should the virus gain the ability to spread person-to-person. analysis.brief_en: Australia is experiencing its first H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza outbreak, confirmed in wild seabirds since June 2026. The virus now threatens iconic and endangered native wildlife, including Tasmanian devils, dingoes, and the platypus, with a government assessment warning nearly one in five of more than 2,000 native species faces high risk. To mitigate impacts, authorities will begin vaccinating captive endangered species such as the orange-bellied parrot and regent honeyeater. While the human health risk is currently assessed as low, the virus has caused over 1,000 human cases globally since the late 1990s, with nearly 50% mortality. Then it arrived – and she saw a tern ‘trembling and swaying’ Volunteers are on the lookout for sick birds as outbreak shatters ‘fairytale belief’ that disease would not reach Australia Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Bird enthusiast Jean Turner hoped avian flu would never arrive at her doorstep. At her home on Kangaroo Island in South Australia, bossy fairy wrens chirp at her from the deck, grey currawongs clumsily fall into her bird bath, and fluffy, hooded plover chicks emerge from speckled eggs in front of her binoculars. But online, images of Argentinian coastlines strewn with dead seal pups and researchers lining up rows of dead seabirds on Antarctic islands offered a warning of what could come. ‘We expected it, but now it’s here’: on the frontline of Australia’s bird flu outbreak, people are distressed Read more So when SA confirmed its first case of the deadly H5 bird flu strain, just over 200km away at Robe on the Limestone Coast, Turner was prepared to become a different kind of birder. “We had this fairytale belief that maybe we wouldn’t get it here,” she says. “But it’s here and now things are going to get harder and more confronting.” She is one of more than 120 volunteers who have signed up for the Bird Observers Network, which allows birders to contribute to the state’s bird flu response. Since the network’s first session, Turner has already reported a sick greater crested tern, which was resting at the edge of a flock. While the other birds shuffled or flew around as she tried to get a better look, the sick animal did not respond. “It was standing on the jetty, trembling and swaying a bit,” Turner says. “It didn’t look well, it just looked really miserable.” Compared with the non-bird-obsessed general public, birders can offer greater detail when reporting potentially infected birds, says Steven Langley, the president of Birds SA. The first mass mortality event of the outbreak was detected last week among greater created terns at Baudin Rocks, just across the beach from Robe, where more than 80 dead and sick birds were spotted. analysis.time: Published on 2026-08-13; event occurred in early August 2026 following South Australia's confirmation of H5 bird flu on 2026-08-07.
analysis.location_and_population: South Australia, Australia; specifically Robe on the Limestone Coast and Kangaroo Island. Affected population includes wild seabirds (greater crested terns), volunteers from the South Australia Bird Observers Network, and local birding communities.
analysis.event: South Australia confirmed its first case of H5 bird flu in wild seabirds, prompting a community-led surveillance response. Volunteers are trained to identify and report sick birds, with confirmed positive results for H5 in multiple crested terns. The event is confirmed by official surveillance and volunteer reports.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: First mass mortality event detected among greater crested terns at Baudin Rocks, with over 80 dead and sick birds reported. Multiple crested terns on Kangaroo Island tested positive for H5 bird flu. The outbreak threatens nearly 400 Australian species, including penguins and dolphins. Risk is described as potentially severe due to the ecological impact on wild bird populations and the broader ecosystem.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The South Australia government, in partnership with conservation groups, has activated a volunteer surveillance network to report sick birds. The public is urged not to touch sick or dead animals and to report them via the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline. Surveillance is ongoing, and other states are considering similar models. Uncertainty remains about the full extent of spread and long-term ecological impact.

analysis.brief_en: South Australia has confirmed its first outbreak of H5 bird flu in wild seabirds, with over 80 dead and sick greater crested terns reported at Baudin Rocks near Robe. The state’s government, alongside conservation groups, has mobilized a volunteer network of birders to monitor and report sick birds, with multiple crested terns on Kangaroo Island testing positive for the virus. Authorities urge the public not to handle sick or dead wildlife and to report sightings to a dedicated hotline. The outbreak threatens nearly 400 Australian species, including penguins and dolphins, raising concerns about ecological damage. While surveillance is active, the full scope of the outbreak remains under investigation.

analysis.brief_en: Indiana’s poultry industry has been declared free of avian influenza after no new highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) cases were detected in commercial flocks since May 2026. The state had previously recorded more HPAI-related flock losses than any other U.S. state in 2026, underscoring the significance of the milestone. The declaration, reported by WATTPoultry.com on August 13, 2026, reflects a sustained period without new infections, though the evidence does not specify case counts, exposure numbers, or the basis for the declaration beyond the absence of new cases. The development follows a broader U.S. trend of limited HPAI activity in commercial poultry during mid-2026.

news.excerpt: Fisheries and Livestock and Agriculture Minister Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid has said vaccines for avian influenza and goat pox developed by the Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute (BLRI) will be ...

news.content: Latest Bangladesh Business World Sports Opinion Politics Diplomacy More E-Paper ☀️ 🌐 English বাংলা Russian Hindi Chinese Trending Presidential Election Gold Price Tarique Rahman US-Iran Talks Saudi-Houthi Conflict × Today's Newspaper Latest World Cup Magazine 2026 Election 2026 Follow Us Print: 14 Aug 2026 Health ‘Avian influenza, goat pox vaccines to be produced commercially’ Daily Sun Report, Dhaka Published: 12 Aug 2026, 12:00 AM Updated: 12 Aug 2026, 03:30 AM Share Share options Print Copy link Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin A A Fisheries and Livestock and Agriculture Minister Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid has said vaccines for avian influenza and goat pox developed by the Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute (BLRI) will be produced commercially and supplied to farmers. He made the remarks as the chief guest at a ceremony at the ministry’s conference room on Tuesday, where BLRI formally handed over the vaccines to the Department of Livestock Services (DLS) for commercial production and wider distribution among farmers. Referring to the livestock sector as an important component of the country’s agricultural economy, the minister said farmers could suffer significant financial losses if diseases affecting poultry and livestock were not controlled. Diseases such as avian influenza, in particular, can have a major impact on poultry production and farm management, he said, stressing the need to strengthen the country’s capacity to develop and produce effective vaccines domestically. The vaccines developed through domestic technology and research would help control diseases in the livestock and poultry sectors, reduce production costs and lessen dependence on imported vaccines, he said. The minister said BLRI scientists and researchers has developed the vaccines using domestic technology and materials after years of research, testing and overcoming various challenges. “If an innovation developed in a laboratory does not benefit ordinary people, the full benefits of that research cannot be realised,” he said, adding that the priority now was to take research-based innovations to commercial production and ensure their use at the farmer level. Highlighting various government initiatives to support agriculture and farmers, the minister said a large number of people in the country were directly or indirectly involved in agriculture. “If agriculture develops, the country’s economy will also become stronger,” he said, adding that the government was working to strengthen farmers and the agricultural sector to advance the overall economy. news.source_body_en: Latest Bangladesh Business World Sports Opinion Politics Diplomacy More E-Paper ☀️ 🌐 English বাংলা Russian Hindi Chinese Trending Presidential Election Gold Price Tarique Rahman US-Iran Talks Saudi-Houthi Conflict × Today's Newspaper Latest World Cup Magazine 2026 Election 2026 Follow Us Print: 14 Aug 2026 Health ‘Avian influenza, goat pox vaccines to be produced commercially’ Daily Sun Report, Dhaka Published: 12 Aug 2026, 12:00 AM Updated: 12 Aug 2026, 03:30 AM Share Share options Print Copy link Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin A A Fisheries and Livestock and Agriculture Minister Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid has said vaccines for avian influenza and goat pox developed by the Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute (BLRI) will be produced commercially and supplied to farmers. He made the remarks as the chief guest at a ceremony at the ministry’s conference room on Tuesday, where BLRI formally handed over the vaccines to the Department of Livestock Services (DLS) for commercial production and wider distribution among farmers. Referring to the livestock sector as an important component of the country’s agricultural economy, the minister said farmers could suffer significant financial losse.

analysis.brief_en: Australia has initiated a vaccination program targeting native birds against H5N1, focusing on captive species at risk of extinction. The move aims to prevent avian influenza outbreaks that could threaten biodiversity. Details on the vaccine formulation, specific bird species prioritized, and implementation timelines remain unclear. Surveillance gaps and uncertainties about the virus's spread among wildlife highlight the need for further research. This proactive measure underscores growing concerns about zoonotic influenza risks in ecosystems.

Every great show needs someone who can hold the room, and for WVC Nashville, that job belongs to Dr. Courtney Campbell, DVM, DACVS-SA. As the conference's official emcee, Dr. Courtney will be the voice guiding attendees through general sessions, big moments on stage, and everything in between at the brand new Music City Center. If you have spent any time on veterinary social media or watched him on national television, you already know he is exactly the right person for the job. New World screwworm has gone from a distant headline to an active concern for veterinarians in the span of a year, and the FDA just handed the profession a new option for fighting it in dogs. On August 13, Zoetis announced that Simparica Trio, its monthly chewable for sarolaner, moxidectin, and pyrantel, received Emergency Use Authorization from the FDA for treating infestations caused by New World screwworm larvae in puppies and dogs. A new study from researchers at the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare adds another intriguing piece to the puzzle. The research suggests that microbes carried into the home by dogs may help reduce respiratory infections during a child's first year of life. Published in Pediatric Allergy and Immunology , the findings suggest that some of the smallest things dogs bring into our homes could have surprisingly big implications for human health. Because choking is a terrifying emergency for pets and their owners, Dr. Christine Rutter , a clinical associa te professor at the Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences , shares what every pet owner and pet sitter should know about r ecognizing choking and responding safely. A second rabid beaver has been confirmed at a Maryland state park just days after another infected beaver was discovered at the same location, prompting officials to close portions of the park and warn visitors who may have been exposed. There's still no licensed bird flu vaccine for dairy cattle. A team at the University of Nebraska just published results that could change that, and the same platform might work in people too. Vampire bats are creeping north out of Mexico. Chronic wasting disease is creeping south out of the Rockies. A prion researcher wants everyone to start thinking about what happens if those two trend lines ever cross, before it becomes a real problem instead of a hypothetical one. Researchers are warning that the country could experience widespread bird deaths and even population declines in some native species after the arrival of the H5N1 2.3.4.4b strain of avian influenza, a virus that has already killed millions of wild birds and marine mammals around the globe. Researchers have identified a Shamonda-like orthobunyavirus , a member of the Simbu serogroup that includes the well-known Schmallenberg virus. While affected cattle are currently experiencing relatively mild illness, veterinary experts are watching closely for a much more concerning possibility: reproductive losses that may not become apparent until the next calving season. There is a reason the veterinary world has been counting down to this one. From August 15 through 18, WVC is stepping outside its longtime Las Vegas home for the very first time and landing in Nashville, Tennessee, at the brand new Music City Center. Discover the best veterinary receptionist continuing education at WVC Nashville. Learn communication, client service, leadership, and burnout prevention. Let's be honest about something. Most CE is not fun. It is necessary, it is important, and the good sessions genuinely make you a better clinician. But the format has not always kept pace with how veterinary professionals actually learn. You sit through a lecture, take notes you may or may not revisit, and walk away hoping something stuck. Every year there are conferences you skip and conferences you wish you had not. WVC Nashville is setting up to be the second kind. There are a lot of veterinary conferences on the calendar every year. Some are good. Some are forgettable. And every once in a while, one comes along that actually changes the conversation. WVC Nashville is shaping up to be that conference for 2026, and if you have not already put it on your radar, this is your sign. 11 careers. 6 questions. Zero chill. Veterinary medicine isn't one job—it's about eleven careers hiding under the same white coat. There is a conversation happening in break rooms, group chats, and parking lots all over veterinary medicine. It usually starts the same way. I love the medicine, but I do not know how much longer I can do this. And it usually ends with a quiet assumption that something is wrong with the person saying it. Somewhere along the way, veterinary medicine developed an unwritten rule: clinical practice is the real job, and everything else is quitting. It gets absorbed in school, reinforced in practice, and carried around as guilt by veterinarians who are exhausted, curious, or simply ready for a change but afraid that stepping out of the exam room means abandoning their oath. If you are graduating this year, the offers are probably already arriving, and some of the numbers are eye-watering. Signing bonuses have become the headline of new grad recruitment, and with student debt where it is, nobody could blame you for reading the biggest number and reaching for a pen. America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dig into the real science, history, and psychology behind humanity's longest-running obsession. We're talking ancient Egypt, where cats were literally worshipped as gods. We're talking the internet, where cats generate more content than almost anything else on the planet. From ancient worship to TikTok stardom, cats have clawed their way into our hearts and honestly, they never asked for permission. But why? What is it about the most indifferent creature on the planet that makes humans absolutely lose their minds? Think black cats bring bad luck? Think again. The truth about black cats is stranger, richer, and way more interesting than the superstition and Caitlin and Clay are here to set the record straight. In this episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dive deep into the wild world of cat mythology, feline folklore, and the weirdest cat superstitions that humans have carried for centuries. We are talking black cats across cultures — feared in some, worshipped in others. We are talking mythological cats from ancient Egypt to Norse legends to the shadowy corners of the internet. We are talking the real history behind the myths that still follow these animals into shelters today, where black cats consistently wait the longest for homes. Spoiler: the cats were never the problem. Think you know everything about cats? In this hilarious episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer takes on the ultimate cat trivia challenge — and her cat daddy husband Clay is putting her knowledge to the test. From quirky cat facts to surprising feline science, this quiz will challenge even the most devoted cat lovers. Play along and see if you can beat America’s favorite veterinary receptionist, Caitlin Palmer! But it's not just fun and games. Every wrong answer comes with a punishment — and that punishment is pickle juice. Yes, really. Watch to find out who walks away victorious and who walks away regretting their cat knowledge gaps. • Fun (and tricky) cat trivia questions • Surprising cat facts you probably didn’t know • A very questionable pickle juice challenge Who’s the ultimate cat nerd... and who’s about to drink pickle juice? In this hilarious episode of Pet Candy, Caitlin and Clay go head-to-head in a cat trivia challenge with a twist—get a question wrong, and you have to take a sip of pickle juice Think you know cats? Play along and see if you can beat them (without the punishment.) Meet Kennedi Robinson, a fourth-year Purdue DVM student building the mentorship and support system she needed. Her grandfather, pioneering veterinarian Dr. Maurice Crouch, paved the way in 1937 as the first Black veterinary graduate of Kansas State University. Now Kennedi is paying it forward, and changing vet med in the process. Meet Dr. Jonnathan Escobar, a first generation Colombian American veterinarian in Houston who never needed a Plan B. A Vet Candy Rising Stars 2026 feature. Rowan University Class of 2030’s Paige Huntzberry is building a career at the intersection of marine science, conservation, and veterinary medicine, one species most people never get to meet at a time. A DVM Candiate at St. George's University School of Veterinary Medicine, Leah Laabs didn't arrive at vet school the way many of her classmates did, fresh off an undergraduate degree with research experience and a letter of recommendation from a favorite professor. She arrived with years already logged on the floor of an emergency veterinary hospital, the kind of experience that doesn't show up cleanly on a transcript but reshapes how a person sees the entire profession. Allison Belaunde is a first-generation Latina veterinarian from Western University, Class of 2026. She is building a career centered on oncology, representation, and opening doors for the next generation. Saya Nei is a UC Davis veterinary student whose dream extends far beyond the exam room, to global outreach, underserved communities, and accessible veterinary care throughout the Middle East. Rachel Lapidus will tell you that if she were not becoming a veterinarian, she would be writing songs. Music is the thing that clears her mind completely, the one place where the noise of clinical rotations and board prep and the relentless pace of veterinary school cannot follow her. It is also, in a way, a window into who she is. Dr. Joya Griffin and Dr. Forrest Cummings just dropped the veterinary CE series that changes how you think about complex cases and it is free with your Vet Candy membership. There are continuing education programs, and then there are continuing education programs where you accidentally debunk a mythical creature between bites of fried dough. This particular offering from Vet Candy lands firmly in the second category. Based on a short story by Vet Candy’s CEO and X-Files super fan, Dr. Jill Lopez. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Dermatology Secrets featuring Dr. Joya Griffin. This three-part online course is designed for veterinarians and veterinary technicians and covers the dermatology skills that matter most in everyday practice — skin cytology, histopathology and biopsy interpretation, and the strangest and most diagnostically challenging cases in specialist dermatology. Learn how to read a cytology slide with confidence, decode a dermatopathology report, and work through complex skin presentations that have not responded to standard treatment. Earn 1.5 RACE CE credits at no cost with your free Vet Candy Membership! Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Unleash Your Inner Hero! , an 8-module urgent care program led by veterinary criticalist Dr. Natosha Richardson. Offering 3.5 RACE CE credits for veterinarians and veterinary technicians, this course covers triage, CPR, supportive care, diagnostics, and treatment across neurologic, gastrointestinal, respiratory, and integumentary emergencies. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with the Respiratory Disease Master Course featuring Criticalist Dr. Anthony Gonzalez. Brought to you by Trudell Animal Health, this 8-module course provides 4 RACE CE credits for veterinarians and veterinary technicians. It covers recognition, diagnosis, and management of acute and chronic respiratory disease, including practical guidance on critical care, advanced monitoring, oxygen therapy, and evidence-based treatment strategies. Designed for immediate clinical application, this course helps veterinary professionals improve outcomes in high-stakes respiratory cases. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Endocrinology Secrets featuring Dr. Forrest Cummings. This online course is designed for veterinarians and veterinary technicians and covers real-world management of diabetes in dogs and cats, Cushing’s disease, and Addison’s disease. Learn how to interpret diagnostics, manage challenging endocrine cases, and improve patient outcomes with practical, case-based guidance. Earn 2 RACE CE credits at no cost—no subscription or credit card required. The Gut-Brain connection is more connected than we thought. This episode of Catching Up explores the fascinating link between the gut and brain in pets. Could your patient's GI issues be tied to behavior? The science says yes. Acute Kidney Injury Alert: New Biomarkers That Could Save Lives. Dr. Elan Armstrong & Dr. Shannon Gregoire break down the newest research on acute kidney injury. World-First Breakthrough: Stem Cells from Cats Could Revolutionize Kidney Disease Treatment! Vet Candy has the details with Dr. Elan & Dr. Shannon. Big news in hemangiosarcoma research! Tune in as we cover a promising breakthrough that could change the way we approach this aggressive cancer. Inside: Dr. Wailani Sung helps you learn how to Recognize the Subtle Signs of Pain in Cats. Presented by Zoetis, maker of Solensia. SolensiaVetTeam.com A cat eye that won't heal is one of those cases that can quietly spiral into something serious — fast. In this episode of Rounds with Dr. Shannon, Dr. Shannon Gregoire sits down with veterinary ophthalmologist Dr. DJ Haeussler for a real clinical conversation about the feline eye cases that challenge general practitioners the most, starting with the corneal ulcer that just won't close. A limping dog walks into your exam room. The owner says it started two weeks ago. The leg looks fine. The X-rays look fine. Nothing adds up — yet. In this episode of Mystery Case Rounds, Dr. Shannon Gregoire walks through a real clinical case of canine lameness from the first exam to the final diagnosis, showing exactly how she thinks through a case when the answer isn't obvious. Veterinary emergency specialist Dr. Kristin Welch walks through a real hyperglycemia case that didn't follow the textbook. Watch the diagnostic reasoning unfold on Vet Candy's Mystery Case Rounds. Dr. Ashley Bourgeois breaks down what is really going on when a Pomeranian loses its coat, the hormonal, genetic, and inflammatory factors may be at play, why this breed is uniquely predisposed to certain dermatologic conditions, and how to build a workup that actually leads somewhere instead of chasing your tail. Nearly a quarter of homeless youth in the U.S. have pets — and some choose veterinary care over their own health care. The Seattle One Health Clinic offers both, side by side, for free. Jeremiah Pouncy shares why this One Health model is changing how we think about the human-animal bond and community care. In Barcelona, scientists are building a biological deep freeze for endangered species, storing genetic material from nearly 300 species and using AI to unlock the future of conservation. Jeremiah Pouncy explains how the Barcelona CryoZoo could change everything we know about saving wildlife from extinction. With fewer than 800 left on Earth, the Bengal florican is one of the rarest birds alive. But in India's Manas National Park, over 800 former poachers have become the species' fiercest protectors. Jeremiah Pouncy tells the remarkable story of how community-led conservation turned a near-extinction into a comeback. A new study on the "Capitoline dolphins" off Rome's coast reveals a population in crisis. Seven out of ten show signs of malnutrition, many bear scars from fishing gear, and scientists warn they may disappear without urgent intervention. Jeremiah Pouncy breaks down what is threatening one of the world's most historically significant dolphin populations and why it matters. Vet Candy's hit podcast recently went live in Nashville, and what started as another fast-paced battle of veterinary knowledge quickly turned into something no one in the room saw coming. Dr. Lauren Downey Koos didn't have to look far to get to WVC Nashville. She works at BluePearl Veterinary in Franklin, Tennessee, which means the conference is essentially in her backyard. She graduated from the University of Florida in 2018, went into neurology, and became a specialist faster than most people finish paying off their student loans. Hosts Caitlin and Clay Palmer, the masterminds behind Vet Candy's trivia and news game show, challenge Carey to a fast-paced reckoning with the week's wildest veterinary headlines, most surprising research breakthroughs, and oddest animal stories circulating through the profession. It's loosely inspired by NPR's Wait Wait... Don't Tell Me, except everyone involved actually knows what a splenectomy is. Veterinary technicians Peter Carlos and Jaycee join Vet Candy's Medical Mysteries to tell the story of a cat with an acutely enlarged abdomen and a diagnosis nobody saw coming. Nat Geo Wild's Dr. Joya Griffin joins Vet Candy's Medical Mysteries to share the strangest dermatology case of her career — a cat with a wound that refused to heal and a diagnosis nobody expected. Vet Candy study guides works like CliffsNotes for a high-yield species. Instead of drowning in a 1,200 page textbook, you get the distilled version: the diseases the exam loves, the clinical signs you must recognize, the diagnostics and treatments you need at your fingertips. Canine, feline, equine, bovine, and beyond, each guide is organized the way your brain actually studies, not the way a reference text is organized. supplementary_news.content: Azernews.Az Friday, August 14, 2026 Login Latest NATION WORLD BUSINESS OIL & GAS ARMENIAN-AZERBAIJANI RELATIONS EDITORIAL ANALYSIS LIFESTYLE EVENTS HEALTHCARE CULTURE SPORTS OUR WRITERS H5N1 spreads across Australia as authorities race to protect vulnerable birds 11 August 2026 11:08 (UTC+04:00) AzerNEWS Staff Read more Australia is preparing to vaccinate vulnerable native bird species kept in captivity as the highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu continues to spread across the country, local media reported on Tuesday. The country has recorded more than 230 confirmed cases of the virus, while authorities last week reported Australia’s first mass wildlife deaths associated with H5N1, according to ABC News. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the vaccination programme would be rolled out across Australia’s states and territories in the coming days. She said authorities could not prevent H5N1 from spreading among wild birds but could take steps to safeguard species considered most vulnerable to the disease. Under the programme, officials will decide which species should receive the vaccine based on their susceptibility to the virus and the potential consequences for conservation efforts. Environment Minister Murray Watt said vaccinating wild birds on a large scale would not be practical because the vaccine requires two doses. However, targeted vaccination of wild birds could be considered where it is logistically possible. The Australian government has initially allocated A$2 million ($1.3 million) for vaccines. Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson said vaccination alone would not be sufficient to control the outbreak, emphasising that strong biosecurity measures would continue to play a key role in limiting the virus’s spread. H5N1 cases have now been confirmed across most of Australia, with Tasmania, the Northern Territory and the Australian Capital Territory the only jurisdictions yet to report infections. Despite the spread among wild birds, authorities have so far found no evidence of H5N1 in poultry or the wider agricultural sector. supplementary_news.content: Bird baths posed similar risks because they draw birds into close contact and can become contaminated if not cleaned regularly, he said. The warning comes as New Zealand continues to monitor the arrival of H5N1 avian influenza following the country’s first two confirmed cases . The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) says there have been no further detections since July 17 and there is no evidence of mass mortality in wildlife or any detection in poultry. Surveillance has been stepped up. Across the Tasman, the situation has escalated in recent weeks, with Australian authorities confirming more than 50 H5N1 detections in wild seabirds across five states, including local transmission among greater crested terns in South Australia and a mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks. Last week, the virus spread beyond coastal species, with Australia’s first land-based bird death confirmed in a magpie in southwest Victoria – marking a significant shift inland in the outbreak’s reach. The risk of H5N1 avian bird flu spreading is greater anywhere birds gather in large numbers. Photo / Sarah Curtis Experts say the disease spreads more rapidly among birds that breed or congregate in dense numbers because the virus spreads rapidly through close contact and contaminated environments. McLean noted that bird feeders were already a vector for disease and need to be cleaned regularly, as bird faeces in and around the food could cause and spread Salmonella infections, avian pox and intestinal parasites. “Large concentrations of birds around garden feeders also cause aggression and this can skew the local diversity of birds in favour of already abundant species.” He said bird enthusiasts could better assist local birds by planting native plants and trees, restoring the environment and controlling pests. “Planting a layered mix of ground covers, shrubs and trees in your garden can provide insects, nectar, fruit, seeds, nesting sites and shelter for many native bird species,” McLean said. The arrival of H5N1 has also prompted concern among pet owners. Wairarapa veterinarian Dr Louisa Broughton told RNZ that while infections in cats are considered rare, H5N1 can have a high mortality rate when it does occur. She said owners concerned about the risk could reduce exposure by keeping cats away from sick or dead birds. Biosecurity Minister Andrew Hoggard has also advised dog owners not to allow pets to eat dead birds found on beaches or elsewhere. Overseas, H5N1 has infected a range of mammals , including cats and dogs, prompting authorities to issue similar warnings. Bird expert Ian McLean says instead of using feeding stations, bird lovers can encourage birds into their gardens by planting species that provide insects, nectar, fruit, seeds, nesting sites and shelter. Photo / Sarah Curtis MPI chief veterinary officer Dr Mary van Andel said the risk to pets in New Zealand remains “very low”, noting that cases overseas have generally occurred in places where the virus is circulating widely in wild birds or other animals. “In rare instances, dogs can become infected, but those that do rarely become seriously unwell,” van Andel said. “They can pick up the virus by mouthing infected birds, so all dogs should be kept away from sick or dead birds and other wildlife.” While it’s similarly rare, cats can also become sick through consuming contaminated animal products such as raw milk. The ministry says pet owners should prevent wild birds from accessing pet food and water; keep dogs on a leash near wild birds, keep cats indoors or discourage hunting behaviour; and ensure pets don’t touch or eat sick or dead animals. Sarah Curtis is a news reporter for the Northern Advocate , focusing on a wide range of issues. She has nearly 20 years’ experience in journalism, most of which she spent reporting on the courts in Gisborne and the East Coast

supplementary_news.content: World Australia to vaccinate birds against H5 avian influenza As of yesterday, authorities have reported there are 231 confirmed or presumed positive detections of H5 bird flu in Australia. — Leanne Buchan/Leanne Buchan Photography handout pic via AFPF Tuesday, 11 Aug 2026 4:17 PM MYT SYDNEY, Aug 11 — Australian authorities said today they would vaccinate bird species deemed to be especially vulnerable to the highly contagious H5 bird flu virus. The country was for years the only continental landmass free of the H5 strain, which has caused severe disease and death in poultry and wild birds worldwide. The first Australian case was discovered in a migratory sea bird in June and last week the government reported its first mass mortality event in wildlife. As part of efforts to protect birds, officials said they would roll out targeted vaccinations for both captive and wild species. “It is difficult to vaccinate birds in the wild — it does take two vaccination doses to vaccinate birds,” environment minister Murray Watt said. “It is difficult to catch wild birds once, let alone twice,” he said. “Where it is possible to vaccinate wild birds, we will do so, but the priority is to vaccinate birds that are in captivity.” Agriculture minister Julie Collins said Australia should expect to see more mass bird deaths. “This will continue to spread across the country,” she said. The wild birds most affected by the H5 strain include waterfowl, shorebirds, seabirds and birds of prey. As of yesterday, authorities have reported there are 231 confirmed or presumed positive detections of H5 bird flu in Australia. There have been no cases detected in poultry or in the country’s agriculture production. Almost half of Australia’s wild bird species, and 83 per cent of its mammals, are found nowhere else. The H5 bird flu strain killed more than 13,000 elephant seal pups after infecting a breeding colony on the remote Heard and McDonald Islands, Australian scientists said in June. — AFP You May Also Like

supplementary_news.content: Asia - Pacific Australia’s New South Wales confirms bird flu cases in native birds Latest cases involve greater crested terns found dead near western New South Wales Islamuddin Sajid 08 August 2026 • Update : 08 August 2026 ISLAMABAD Australia’s New South Wales government has confirmed two new cases of H5 avian influenza in native birds, bringing the state’s total to four, ABC News reported Saturday, citing an official government statement. The latest cases involved greater crested terns found dead near Narooma on the south coast and Wentworth in western New South Wales. The birds were reported by members of the public and tested by the state’s H5 response team. The first two New South Wales cases were detected in migratory petrels near Port Stephens in July. Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said the detections were not unexpected and the government was prepared to manage further impacts. Authorities are continuing surveillance in affected areas, while the government works with the poultry industry to strengthen biosecurity. No H5 cases have been detected in New South Wales poultry so far. Australian Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson said Friday that testing had confirmed another 20 positive detections in Victoria state, all involving greater crested terns in the Portland and Nelson area. Australia has now recorded 175 confirmed or presumed positive H5 bird flu detections based on tested samples. However, authorities said there had been no detections in poultry or Australia’s agricultural production system, while the risk to humans remained very low. Concerns have also prompted the Royal Adelaide Show to cancel bird and poultry exhibits scheduled for next month. supplementary_news.content: Beef Cattle Stories Free Newsletter Digital Editions Subscribe Home News Markets Markets news Market Prices Crops Crop Management Oil Seeds Canola Canola Guide Soybeans Sunflowers Flax Cereals Wheat Barley Oats Corn Pulses Soybeans Chickpeas Field Crops Potatoes Potato Guide Livestock Livestock Sales Beef cattle Calf Central Herd Health Livestock Sales Weather FarmLife Machinery AgDealer Classifieds Events Ag in Motion Beef Cattle Stories Proudly Canadian Home News Markets Markets news Market Prices Crops Crop Management Oil Seeds Canola Canola Guide Soybeans Sunflowers Flax Cereals Wheat Barley Oats Corn Pulses Soybeans Chickpeas Field Crops Potatoes Potato Guide Livestock Livestock Sales Beef cattle Calf Central Herd Health Livestock Sales Weather FarmLife Machinery AgDealer Classifieds Events Ag in Motion Free Newsletter Digital Editions Subscribe Proudly Canadian Dairy Cattle Advertissement Researchers can’t yet tell if viruses drift from manure tankers USDA researchers put air samplers six metres from a spreading tanker and found only the bacterial marker By William DeKay 2 days ago 6 min read Researchers have traced the spillover of H5N1 avian influenza virus into U.S. dairy cattle. Photo: File When highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza spread into U.S. dairy cattle, it raised the pressing question for farmers and regulators: what happens when virus‐contaminated dairy manure is spread on fields? That’s the focus of new research led by Dr. Tucker Burch of the USDA Agricultural Research Service. Why It Matters Poultry farms have tested positive shortly after nearby dairies spread manure. Nobody has proven a link, and proving one requires knowing whether viruses actually travel in the aerosol when a tanker is running. Why the lagoon became the question Burch spoke at an international conference about avian influenza, held in partnership with the University of Guelph. He outlined how viral and fecal bioaerosols are spread during dairy manure application. “The background here is the spillover of H5N1 into U.S. dairy cattle. This is a very novel challenge for the dairy industry. The virus was shed during this outbreak at very high titer in the milk. A lot of that actually ends up in the manure lagoons,” said Burch. In a study by Emory University, the avian influenza virus was found at multiple California dairy farms in several locations, including manure lagoons. That raised questions about manure management. Read Also Dairy Cattle The milk never leaves the farm, but it still moves through quota “Because it’s in the lagoon, there were lots of questions that came up,” said Burch. “What do we do with this waste? It needs to get land applied. Do we need to hold onto it for a certain amount of time (or) can it get applied right away? And then, during application, are there any concerns with aerosols drifting away from the application site?” There was added urgency to these questions after anecdotal reports of poultry farms that tested positive shortly after nearby dairy farms had spread manure. That suggested aerosols could be involved, even if the link hadn’t been proven. A decade of practice at catching things in the air Burch works in a joint USDA–USGS laboratory in central Wisconsin that operates closely with the University of Wisconsin Marshfield Agricultural Research Station, which has a dairy farm that milks about 120 cows and raises 400 to 500 heifers. He describes the farm as an ideal research partner. The research team has relevant experience. Nearly a decade ago, when Wisconsin dairies explored irrigation-based manure spreading using centre pivots and traveling guns, nearby residents worried those systems might spray zoonotic pathogens into the air. Burch’s group sampled the air for micro-organisms to assess risk. “If you’re collecting air samples to look at micro-organisms, there’s essentially three types of technology. You can impact the organisms on a solid media, you can impinge them in a liquid media, or you can filter them out,” he said. The process involved cumbersome gear including pumps, generators and extension cords. “To collect air samples for one hour, we usually spent two hours just moving equipment around.” In early 2024, as the dairy H5N1 outbreak unfolded, Burch encountered a battery‐operated air sampler made by NovaPrep (the cub sampler) that runs at very high flow rates, which means high concentration of material on a filter. What turned up inside the barns His team obtained several units and quickly put them to work at the research farm. Samples were taken in the milking parlour, dairy barn, heifer barn and transition barn for new arrivals, as well as at outdoor locations. Burch said he quickly learned how easily outdoor controls can be contaminated if placed too close to barns. Samples were analyzed for a suite of indigenous enteric viruses and for ruminant bacteroides, a bacterial marker in cattle feces. Patterns matched animal age groups. “We detected a variety of viruses on the farm and found some interesting and sensible correlations with probably the age of the livestock we were sampling,” said Burch. Bovine polyomavirus was found more often in the milking parlor, and both adenovirus and enterovirus were associated with younger animals. He said ruminant bacteroides appeared in every indoor air sample, although concentrations varied. Six metres from the tanker U.S. Department of Agriculture researchers are looking into what happens when virus‐contaminated dairy manure is spread on fields. The ongoing study is motivated from a 2024 outbreak of H5N1 avian influenza detected in U.S. dairy cattle. Photo: File Burch’s team wanted to test air during tanker-based manure application, so it ran a trial in 2025 in an approximately 400‐metre field. Samplers were set as close as six metres from the spread area. Manure samples from the tankers showed high levels of ruminant bacteroides, bovine adenovirus, coronavirus and enterovirus. In the downwind air, only the bacterial marker (ruminant bacteroidetes) appeared. Making sure tests are correct Although tests are more sensitive than they were in the past, there is still concern about adequate virus detection. Naturally occurring viruses in manure are too sparse and variable to serve as reliable tracers so the team is adding high concentrations E. coli into the tankers and tracking them downwind. The team is now planning to use coliphage (a type of bacteriophage) as a spiked viral marker in manure tankers. By adding large quantities of coliphage (approximately 100 quadrillion plaque-forming units of coliphage), they hope to create a detectable signal in downwind air samples, allowing for more powerful assessment of viral aerosolization and transport. Sampling the lagoon itself During his presentation, Burch credited Dr. Joseph Heffron, also from the USDA, for this plan B approach. Heffron also spoke at the conference about sampling methods for surveillance of livestock viruses in a dairy manure lagoon, with a particular focus on avian influenza and other enteric viruses. Heffron’s study, also at a University of Wisconsin Marshfield agricultural research station, used a two-stage lagoon system where the primary five-million-litre lagoon overflows into a secondary four-million-litre lagoon. Sampling strategies included perimeter sampling, centre-of-lagoon sampling using specialized lake samplers, and large-volume filtered samples from the secondary lagoon. He said lagoons are not only a potential source of environmental contamination when manure is land-applied, but also serve as important monitoring points for assessing herd health. “This is really the motivation of coming to, and this is the question that I want to answer, is how do we get from something that is tens of millions of litres down to six microlitres of template that we put into our PCR (polymerase chain reaction),” he said. While the recent study remains ongoing, key data findings so far include: What the lagoon sampling shows so far Sample the interior, not the edge. Virus concentrations are consistently higher in the lagoon interior than at the perimeter, so perimeter sampling alone is not sufficient. Do not agitate first. Agitating the lagoon increases fecal bacteria signals but marginally reduces virus detection, so agitation is not helpful when the goal is finding viruses. Replicate at every step. Multiple locations, multiple samples and multiple extractions are all important for reliable detection. supplementary_news.content: Friday 14 August, 2026 Archive বাংলা HOME News PM President Top News National Arts & Entertainment July Uprising Education News Health News Climate Change & Environment Science & Technology Weather Business International District Interview Sports Notun Kuri Sports Subscriber NOTICE All News News Flash PM urges US companies to invest confidently, build long-term businesses in Bangladesh PM’s India, Japan visits not finalised yet: Shama PM pledges support to expand mathematics Olympiad at grassroots BNP submits nomination paper for Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir in presidential election Mirza Fakhrul set to hold highest constitutional position from grassroots News BSS 11 Aug 2026, 18:50 Update : 11 Aug 2026, 19:15 BLRI vaccines for avian flu, Gumboro disease handed over for commercial production: Rashid Photo: PID DHAKA, Aug 11, 2026, (BSS) - Vaccines for avian influenza and Gumboro disease developed by the Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute (BLRI) have been formally handed over to the Department of Livestock Services (DLS) for commercial production and expansion at the farmers’ level, said Fisheries and Livestock Minister Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid. “The vaccines, developed through indigenous technology and research, would play an important role in controlling diseases in the country’s poultry sector, reducing production costs and decreasing dependence on imports,” he said. He made the remarks at a vaccine handover ceremony held today at the conference room of the ministry at the secretariat here. Senior officials of the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock, director general of the Department of Livestock Services and Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute, scientists and researchers, university teachers and veterinarians, industry entrepreneurs, representatives of farmers and representatives of vaccine-producing companies attended the programme. Director General of the Department of Livestock Services Md. Shahnewaz Khan and Director General of the Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute Dr. Shakila Faruk, among other officials, were also present. Rashid said today’s event was not merely a formal handover of vaccines, but an important step towards taking knowledge and innovations achieved in laboratories to farmers at the field level. BLRI scientists and researchers developed the two vaccines using indigenous technology through years of research, testing and trials despite various challenges, he added. He said an invention completed in a laboratory cannot deliver its full benefit unless it is brought into practical use for ordinary people. Therefore, he said, the priority now is to take research-based innovations to the stage of commercial production and ensure their use at the farmers’ level. The minister said the BLRI-developed vaccines for avian influenza and Gumboro disease had been handed over to the Department of Livestock Services for commercial production. This has opened a new window of opportunity for the country’s poultry sector, he said, adding that if the concerned institutions work in coordination, it will be possible to make the vaccines available to farmers within a short time. He congratulated all scientists, researchers, officials and employees of BLRI involved in developing the vaccines, as well as those concerned with the Department of Livestock Services. He particularly expressed gratitude to those who worked in laboratories for a long time and contributed to developing the vaccines through testing and trials using indigenous technology and materials. At the programme, the minister also highlighted various government initiatives aimed at supporting agriculture and farmers. The country’s economy will also improve with the development of agriculture, he said, adding that the government is working to advance the overall economy by strengthening farmers and agriculture. Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid said the farmers’ economy would become stronger if they received fair prices for their products. Improvement in the economic condition of farmers would have a positive impact on the national economy, he said. As Bangladesh is an agriculture-based country, he said, agriculture needs to be further strengthened as one of the major driving forces of the economy in the coming days. Referring to the financial difficulties faced by farmers, the minister said the government has taken initiatives to resolve the longstanding loan-related problems of small and marginal farmers. He said loans of up to Taka 10,000 taken by small and marginal farmers who had faced difficulties in repaying them had been waived. The minister said the banks concerned did not suffer losses due to the loan waiver, as the government paid the banks the amount on behalf of the farmers. As a result, the farmers’ debt burden was reduced while the lending banks also received their dues, he said. Referring to various agriculture-based government programmes, he said initiatives including Family Card, Farmer Card and canal excavation programmes had been undertaken. He said the drainage system had weakened as canal excavation activities had remained largely suspended for a long time. As a result, even slight excessive rainfall caused waterlogging and sudden flooding in various areas. The minister said the government has adopted a five-year plan to revive canals across the country. Under the plan, excavation of designated canals is being carried out every year. The Ministry of Agriculture and other relevant departments are working according to their respective responsibilities. He said around 90 percent of canal excavation work under the Ministry of Agriculture had already been completed this year. The government institutions assigned with responsibilities must not merely show progress on paper, but prove progress through actual work, he added. Highlighting the importance of the Farmer Card in ensuring production and fair prices for farmers, the minister said the card would play an important role in providing farmers with advance information on which products would bring them greater profits at a particular time, which products are in demand in the market and what kind of assistance is required for production. Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid said farmers would also be provided with more effective support, from supplying necessary production inputs, including fertiliser and seeds, to ensuring fair prices for their products. He said if accurate information is delivered to farmers at the right time, production planning would become more effective and the risk of unnecessary supply shortages or overproduction in the market could be reduced. The minister also said registration for the Farmer Card was progressing rapidly. So far, registration of around 1.3 million farmers has been completed, he added. Although the government has a three-year plan for the programme, efforts are being made to complete the Farmer Card registration process ahead of the stipulated timeframe, he said. The minister said the livestock sector is also an important part of the country’s agricultural economy. If diseases in the poultry and livestock sectors are not controlled, farmers may face substantial financial losses, he said.
